Part I · The Realm at a Glance · Section 01 of 15

Overview

Dating. Vysoans reckon the years from the birth of the Founder, Āelyxanthor . Years after it are given as RŌĀ, Rȳarl Ōsare Āeksys, "Year of Our Lord"; years before it as ÑĀ, Ñesīr Āelyxanthor, "Before Āelyxanthor." Year 1 RŌĀ is the year of his birth; there is no year 0. The present date is RŌĀ 1017. Sources. Much of what follows draws on House Vēzgharyōñ's own private annals rather than any crown-licensed history, unratified by the College of Jehābari, and coloured throughout by the house's own reading of its past — not least its conviction that the gift by which the Zaldrāeksi of old bonded their dragons runs in its blood still, and was given for a purpose.

Vysos is the fourth of seven worlds orbiting the star Vēzos, a system of the Infinitas Galaxy that its people have only this year learned to leave. It is the seat of House Vēzgharyōñ, whose Thirty-Eight Kings have held it without interruption for close on a thousand years, from the Navigator Āelyxanthor , who raised the Black Tower at Zobrezos in RŌĀ 36, down to Āeñāriōñ , who ascended in RŌĀ 1017.

Some seven billion Vysoans live on Vysos itself, with a small colony on Vēzperzyon and the crews of the system's extraction stations besides, governed as a sacral absolute monarchy: an unaccountable sacred crown set above the Nineteen Chairs and a restricted-franchise legislature, the Gerialbar, whose commons sit in the Qupteōrion beneath the noble Āeksiōrion. In RŌĀ 1017 the realm's own engineers, under Āedāriōñ , brought the first hyperdrive to working order — a breakthrough of Vysos's own making, salvaged from no one and given by no one, at the end of a climb the house has made alone for close on a thousand years — and in the same year the throne passed to Āeñāriōñ , who inherits a realm able, for the first time, to reach beyond its own star.

Vysos stands at the edge of a galaxy it has never met. No other people has yet been found among the stars, and everything the realm understands of itself it worked out at home. What its own oldest histories call magic and monster and mystery — dragonfire, the visions of the seers of the flame, the bond by which the Zaldrāeksi of Valiērīa rode their dragons — is now understood as the work of the gift: the psionic latency carried by a share of its people, long before the realm had a word for it other than wonder. Nothing about the house's own past changes under that understanding. Only what it is taken to mean does. What the throne means to become beyond Vēzos it has already set down as its stated aims — waystation, financial haven, archive and escort to whatever it finds there.

The Vēzos System#

Vēzos is an unremarkable star save for one fact: it keeps seven worlds in its light. Only the fourth, Vȳsōs, was ever asked to carry a people.

OrderWorldNatureMoonsPopulation

The system's people number roughly seven billion, nearly all of them on Vȳsōs; the colony on Vēzperzyon, founded under Vēzāerys , is small still, and the other worlds carry only the crews of the extraction stations set on them in the same reign. The seven worlds carry names inherited from Valiērīa, which ruled long before this house claimed a throne — each named, in the order its star-watchers found them, for a god the Valiērii held dear, Vēzperzyon first among them. Until RŌĀ 1017 no Vysoan vessel had ever left the light of Vēzos, and no other people has yet been met beyond it.

Time is kept by the Kēlāeriōñ Calendar, set down under Kēlāeriōñ with the Eglābaros and the College of Jehābari and unaltered since: a Vēziñ (day) of 24 Arlēdi (hours); a Sīkōz (week) of 7 Vēziñi; a Hūrarl (month) of 4 Sīkōzi; a Rȳarl (year) of 13 Hūrarli plus one extra day, the Jemēsiñ Vēzose, kept apart at the year's start as the turning of winter into spring. The Rȳarl it keeps is the world's orbit, and the seasons were not always so obliging: through the realm's earliest centuries winters and summers alike ran long and lawless, as the oldest annals record them, a disorder the house now reads as the long shadow of the Cataclysm, whose ash hung in the sky for generations after Valiērīa's fall. As the world settled, the seasons steadied with it, until by Kēlāeriōñ 's reign they kept near enough the orbit's turning that the Jemēsiñ Vēzose could be set down as winter's end without falsehood.

Origins — a Native People#

Three foundational truths, entered in the order they are old rather than the order the house learned them. None needs correcting; each is set down here plainly, apart from the legend that has grown around it.

The Vysoans are native to Vȳsōs in the plain sense — not seeded, not marooned, simply born of this world and of no other. They are a fair people: silver-blonde of hair, with eyes that run from lilac to the darkest purple. They kept no written memory of their own beginning, and none survives to recover.

The gift runs in a share of them and not in the rest. The psionic-latent among the Vysoans — the gifted — can move things unseen, speak mind to mind, walk abroad apart from the body, and scry what lies far off or ahead, the flame-seeing of the old seers among it. The realm's oldest histories call this magic. It is by the gift that the Zaldrāeksi bonded their dragons, and by the gift that they achieved the other feats their annals record.

The dragons are native fauna of Vȳsōs, as much a part of its wild as any other great beast, and no one's making. Unbonded, they answer to no one; bonded through the gift, they become the rider's will made flesh and fire. The royal dragons of House Vēzgharyōñ descend from the bonded dragons of Valiērīa.

Valiērīa and the Zaldrāeksi#

Valiērīa, "Land of the Proven Ones," was one of the oldest civilizations of early Vȳsōs, and it lasted for thousands of years. Its people, the Valiērii, were ruled by the Zaldrāeksi, the Dragonlords — a lord among them a Zaldrāeksys, a lady a Zaldrāeksyñ — of whom there were forty families, House Vēzgharyōñ among them. Valiērīa grew from a small city state into an empire over its first few centuries, and its dragons carried that empire further than any power of the world before it. What the Valiērii called the Zaldrāeksi's sorcery — the binding of dragons, the reading of flame, the rule of bloodline over bloodline — was the gift, drawn out and kept close within forty houses and shaped into rite and law.

The Cataclysm#

Valiērīa fell when its capital and core were destroyed in a geological cataclysm: the earth broke beneath the heart of the empire, and fire, ash and sea took in a season what the Zaldrāeksi had built over thousands of years. Of the forty families, House Vēzgharyōñ was one of the lucky few to survive. What remained of the old heartland is the shattered Valiērian peninsula, left unfit to live on for centuries, until Rāethor cleansed it with Scion adepts and Valkarōz founded Arlȳria upon it.

Much of what Valiērīa knew died with its core, and what it did not take, the scattering after it did. Organic technological development is slow because a civilization must derive its own physics before building from it, and the Cataclysm left no working answer behind to copy. Everything Vysos has since built, from the first harnessed steam to the hyperdrive of RŌĀ 1017, it derived again for itself. Timing decides how well each advance is used: worked out before the knowledge that should carry it, an invention stays a curiosity no one can yet build upon; worked out once a realm has already reached something like its own industrial floor, it becomes a step a trained hand can take. House Vēzgharyōñ's long habit of treating whatever its own people invent or rediscover by their own effort as something to be tested, taught and built upon, never feared, is precisely the disposition such a climb needs from whoever leads it — as told more fully under History.

Valenton and the Pryjatājoni#

After the fall, the remnants of the empire split among several city states. At times they formed alliances or blocs, but always on the basis of convenience, and none ever formed a cohesive polity on the scale of its predecessor. Āelyxanthor began his life in Valenton, one of the largest of them. According to the Covenant's teaching, he was born of a virgin maiden of House Vēzgharyōñ, an event made possible by the Sētegqēlosiēr, the Starshaper; and in the Covenant's founding legend it is the Sētegqēlosiēr who directs him to establish a city upon the Pryjatājoni, the Shattered Islands. There, in RŌĀ 36, he laid the foundations of Zobrezos and raised the Black Tower, and from that single city the realm began.

For what the gift, the dragons and the Valiērian bloodline mean under the Sidereal Covenant's own doctrine, see Doctrine & Religion.

The Thirty-Eight Kings — the narrative spine#

Every reign from the Navigator, Āelyxanthor , to the present throne, father to son by default, breaking eight times to a brother, nephew, uncle, or cousin. Gold marks the Founder, red the eight lateral breaks, violet the present king. Each king lives the natural span of his people and no more: Vysoan kings die in their seventies and eighties, as Vysoans ordinarily do, or sooner by war or murder, and only one, Rāeōñ , who came late to the throne after his brother, outlived his own century.

The succession law is primogeniture with an agnatic preference: the crown passes to sons before daughters, and only once the male line closest to the throne is exhausted does it reach sideways for a brother, nephew, uncle, or cousin, exactly as the breaks above show it doing in practice; a daughter's son inherits only when no male-line heir remains, as Auriōñ did through Āelyxaena. A Kardārlisyñ carries her father's blood and royal style, and may carry a claim to her sons, but does not herself take the throne. Nor does the Crown recognize abdication or retirement — where a subject customarily lays down his work at seventy, a Kardārys reigns for the whole of his natural life, however long it runs. Only outright incapacity opens the throne to a regency, and even then the crown does not change hands: a regent — the King's spouse first, failing her his son, and failing both the male heir presumptive — rules in his stead until he recovers or, failing that, until his death passes the crown forward by the same law that has always governed it.

The Imperial Family, RŌĀ 1017#

The reigning house as it stands at RŌĀ 1017. The Succession column numbers each holder's place in the line as the agnatic preference reckons it; a dash marks a member of the family who carries the royal style but holds no numbered place in that line, daughters foremost among them, whose claim reaches only a son and only once the male line has failed. Āezāerys's own twins, Āelyxanthor and Āelyxaena, complicate "eldest" in a way an ordinary birth order never has to — Āelyxanthor is numbered first here only because a decision must be made somewhere, and whether Vysoan law actually resolves such a case remains open.

The household's own names bear out a wider Vysoan custom: a name passes down by its root rather than whole, a family of sound rather than one name repeated past bearing, exactly as the throne's own succession does. Āeñāriōñ 's "Āe-" root runs through Āezāerys to Āelyxanthor, but a second son standing clear of any near claim to the crown need not carry it at all — hence Elaethor, born this year and named for no near ancestor. The cadet lines echo it at smaller scale: Jaehaekarys's root passes to Jaemos, while his second son Raemos takes a rhyme on his uncle's root; Raehaerys's root passes to Raeon. Daughters follow a gentler version — a common cadence across Coranne, Visanne, Jaenanne, and Gelyssa, and an aunt's syllable sometimes lent outright to a niece, as Coranne's is to Coralaena. What the succession law does formally, the family does informally: a name is graded by how close to the crown it sits.

A Vysoan name carries one further mark besides its root and its house: a patronymic, naming the bearer's own father, set between given name and family name and formed the same way any genitive is — the father's name with the suffix -e added to it. Prince Āelyxanthor's full style shows it plainly: Āelyxanthor Āezāeryse Vēzgharyōñ — Āelyxanthor, of Āezāerys, of House Vēzgharyōñ. The custom runs through every rank of society, not the nobility alone; what changes by occasion is how much of the name is used, from the given name alone in everyday address up to the full three-part style reserved for a birth entry, a marriage contract, or a treaty's own signature.

The Reigning Generation#

Āeñāriōñ , thirty-eighth of the line, rides the golden dragon Vēzaēksion and has reigned only since this year, succeeding at one-and-fifty on the death of his father Āedāriōñ at eighty-one — in the very year his father's engineers brought the realm's first hyperdrive to working order. At 51 he stands in the full middle of a Vysoan's natural span; a cerebral, history-loving king, he sponsored Vysoan culture and scholarship heavily through his long years as Kardārilaros and means to go on doing so from the throne. He watched the drive come to working order across his father's last years and doubts whether the realm yet understands what it has opened; in the first months of his reign the armed forces have been settled into the configuration they now hold, and while the first drive-fitted hulls are building on the slips the throne holds to caution, sending nothing beyond Vēzos it cannot bring home again.

Kardāryñ Jaenanne Qelosiñe, of the prominent House Qelosiñe, has been his wife these eight-and-twenty years, a match of love as much as calculation, met while both were students. A pillar of the family's stability and his regular counsel on matters of state, she has raised every child of the marriage well and, with the first grandchildren now come, has begun to take up her place as the family's matron.

Kardārilaros Āezāerys, heir to the throne and rider of the red dragon Melqelos, was seven-and-twenty when his father took the crown this year, and holds the Kardārlītsion Zaldrīzedōre, the heir's own principality, alongside his office. A fully-trained Solar Scion as every imperial prince is, his place as heir asked a military career of him besides — ten years in the Vysoan Navy, entered at seventeen, have brought him to Hārvesqogror Valbartos, Captain 3rd Class, in command of a Solsētegȳz of the home fleet. He shares his father's caution toward a galaxy no Vysoan has yet seen, but privately would welcome the chance to see Vysoan space grow wider.

Kardārilēsyñ Elaenyra Ūndembreys, of House Ūndembreys, was born with the rare gift of visions and trained as an Ūndissaryñ — the one member of the immediate imperial family whose place among the Solar Scions rests on her own gift rather than Vēzgharyōñ blood. Matched to Āezāerys at two-and-twenty, he then four-and-twenty, theirs is a marriage warm but dutiful before all else; she is the family's most committed traditionalist, and means to raise her own children to be the same.

Era-by-Era Chronicle#

Vysoan history moves slowly by the measure of most peoples, and the dragons are the reason. A crown that commands the sky on dragonback, and can carry its will across a continent in a day, has never felt the urgency that drives other realms to engines; every advance the Vysoans made, they made without the spur of need, and so they made it late and made it thoroughly.

I. The Gathering of the Isles — RŌĀ 36–253

From the Founder's single city upon the Pryjatājoni, two centuries of gathering rather than invention. Baeriōñ "the Black" brings the neighbouring city states to heel; Āelyxanthor 's marriage folds Āerakīs into the realm and plants a succession crisis between his elder daughter Āelyxaena and his elder son Āeñāriōñ , whose twenty-eight-year civil war nearly bleeds the line white. The throne passes, for want of any closer candidate, to Auriōñ "the Golden," Āelyxaena's son. His son Auriōs "the Admirable" turns the old royal council into the Gerialbar, a proper parliament. His grandson Aurys dies suppressing a thirteen-year, Braedhōs-backed revolt in Pelarton, and the crown passes sideways for the first time, to his brother Dāeriōñ "the Daring," who ends the war with negotiation rather than more bloodshed — the house's first real experiment in ruling by something other than the sword.

II. The Reign of the Seven Els — RŌĀ 253–416

Ēlyāegon "the Enlightened," inheriting from his uncle in a second lateral break, consolidates rather than conquers, takes for the crown the style of Kardārys, Great King, and sees steam power first harnessed in his reign. He and the six of his line who follow him — the Reign of the Seven Els — preside over steam's slow spread, the growth of the cities, and the realm's first written guarantee of the commons' dignity. Braedhōs is finally absorbed under Ēlyrōz . Prince Ēlythor, blown off course exploring west, discovers the continent named Ēlythoros for him; crowned Ēlythor "the Mariner," he founds Dārilardōr, its first permanent settlement. His son Ēlyāegon convenes the Great Council (RŌĀ 380–390), relaxing lèse-majesté and striking the Covenant's adultery, apostasy, and false-prophecy laws from the books; Ēlyrōz "the Erudite" founds the Maegysombāzmion at Uēpoktio, ties the franchise to its graduates, and raises the Great Library beside it.

III. The Shaping of the Realm — RŌĀ 416–589

The last of the Els, Ēlythel , dies young and without a son, and his uncle Kēlāethor spends the whole of an eight-year reign putting down the princelings who contest the crown — two of whom live on as the founders of Houses Vēzembar and Vēzāegen. His son Kēlāerys sets the realm's names on the three ancient continents — Endāros, Ñāqos, Rōvuēsos — and charts a new southern landmass, Zīrtos. His son Kēlāeriōñ "the Great" gives the realm the institutions it still keeps: he establishes the Solar Scions as a standing institution of the crown, sets down the Kēlāeriōñ Calendar, founds the first Sētegombāzmioni and Botȳsombāzmioni beside the Maegysombāzmion, and codifies the tri-pathway of schooling by which every Vysoan is still taught. His only son, Prince Āethel, is killed by Sȳndorian raiders on the eastern marches in the last years of the reign, and when the old king dies at eighty-one the crown passes to his brother Rāeōñ , already seventy-two. The house's first war against Sȳndorīa, fought by Rāeōñ I in vengeance for his nephew's death, wins nothing but its own name; his son Rāethor "the Restorer" turns the realm's strength homeward instead, cleansing the shattered Valiērian peninsula with Scion adepts, and Rāethel answers with the first aerial vehicles — late, since no engine yet flew as well as a dragon — and claims Ūlthos for its rubber.

IV. The Making of One Vysos — RŌĀ 589–829

Valkariōñ "the Venerable" wins outright against Sȳndorīa and wins the peace besides: High Valiērian is renamed High Vysoan, the common speech becomes Common Vysoan, and a single Vysoan identity is deliberately built over the realm's older peoples. Valkarys formally claims Zīrtos, and close on two centuries of prosperity and a quiet arms race follow: Valkariōñ begins the resettlement of Valiērīa, Valkarōz codifies the Scions' rule and founds the city of Arlȳria on the cleansed peninsula, and under Valkariōñ the nobility receives the Āeksiōrion, drawing the peerage's political teeth. The long peace ends under Vēzāerys . Vēzāeriōñ "the Magnificent" then fights the final war against Sȳndorīa — devastating, total, and final: its heartland is absorbed, its great cities Qelendie and Sȳndoval with it, and the king takes the style of the first Dārysdāri, King of Kings, and formalises the governance of the whole realm under one order.

V. The Ascent — RŌĀ 829–958

With no rival left on Vȳsōs, the realm turns upward. Under Vēzāerys the first rudimentary thinking machines are built and Vysoans begin handing simple processes to them, and the realm is divided for the first time into Vȳse, regional governances standing between the crown and the provinces. His son Vēzāeriōñ "the Stargazer" puts the first foothold on Vysos's own moon, and Vēzāerys plants the colony on Vēzperzyon and the first extraction stations across the Vēzos system. Vēzāethor and Vēzāelyx hold what their fathers built, and when Vēzāelyx I dies at sixty without a son, the crown passes in RŌĀ 958 to his brother.

VI. The Threshold — RŌĀ 958–1017

That brother, Āeñāriōñ , builds the crown a new seat of government — the government island, its mount, its Hall of State, the Great Hall of the People, the Barsīvōñ, and the fifteen Magistracy spires — and gathers the colony on Vēzperzyon and the system's extraction stations under a single Vȳse governed from the new island, taking for the throne the threefold style Trēsyvēzos, Gīmēperzys Nūmāzmēre, Zaldrīzēr Dorāzmēre. The mount's works stand finished within some twenty years of his accession; the wider island is not wholly settled until a decade and more beyond, into his son's reign. The rotunda of the new palace's hall of state, beneath the dome and before the throne, is ringed, from that reign on, with a gilded sun-gold likeness of every king since Āelyxanthor — cast at each king's own accession, a second commissioned at his own discretion, and a reign of real achievement often recast posthumously, the ring always showing whichever likeness has become the most promulgated rather than simply the newest.

Under his son Āedāriōñ the realm's own engineers take up the last problem the Ascent left them: not how to reach the edge of the Vēzos system, which the extraction stations already prove, but how to pass beyond it. No vessel fell from the sky to show them the way, and no stranger came to teach it; the drive was worked out at the Maegysombāzmion and in the crown's own yards from first principles, by a people that had never seen another's. It took the whole of the reign. The theory was settled in its first decade, the first drive that held together under test in its second, and the remaining years went on making it hold reliably enough to trust a crew to it — a labour the old king followed from the throne as closely as any engineer, and lived just long enough to see finished.

In RŌĀ 1017 a single test vessel, crewed by volunteers of the Navy, left the Vēzos system on the new drive and came home again from beyond the reach of its own star, the first Vysoans ever to see Vēzos from outside its light. Āedāriōñ I died within months of their return, at eighty-one, and the throne passed in the same year to Āeñāriōñ , the first king of Vysos to reign over a people able to leave their own sky — and, with that, the first to wonder who else might be out there to meet them.

The Reliquaries of Memory#

Vysoans of great significance may be honoured with a Reliquary of Memory. Into it are set, by the gift, the honoured one's thoughts, teachings and methods, and with them, naturally, a fragment of the personality. A Reliquary is static. It answers only from the knowledge with which it was made, and takes in no new ideas, so that it stands as a timestamp: a memory of the perception, belief and wisdom held at one particular point in Vysoan history. That is its principal purpose, for the realm's living archives hold far more, and are far more current, than any Reliquary can.

Every Kardārys is necessarily so honoured, so that the wisdom each held at the particular point of his rule is preserved. The practice could begin only once the method was possible, and it began with the establishment of the Solar Scions as a standing crown institution under Kēlāeriōñ (r. RŌĀ 455–484); the kings before him are known only by statue, chronicle and record. The Solar Scions alone make the Reliquaries, by the gift, alongside the written and recorded archives in which the realm preserves its other honoured dead.

The Realm Remade — Starsteel Grown Over Stone#

At the Threshold (RŌĀ 1017). Zobrezos has grown vertically for close on a millennium — starsteel-frame towers over black-quarried stone — while its ancient center-isle (the Black Tower, the Wyrmcove, the Sunbeacon) stays inviolate by decree, modernized internally but unchanged in outward form. The city has spread across most of the Pryjatājoni, merged with the neighbouring city states Baeriōñ first brought to heel into one metropolis, and absorbed two old Āerakii towns as suburbs. Three older towns at a great river's mouth in Endāros have merged into Dārlinion; three older cities on a great bay of Ñāqos into Ghisazma; Braedhōs, Pelarton, and two of their neighbours into Dāervesālion. On Rōvuēsos, the colonial port of Vējōzos has become the great city of the south since medicine overcame the disease and terrain that doomed earlier colonization.

How it grew. Growth ran deliberately unhurried through the Ascent, the crown preferring cities that thickened in place to cities that sprawled, then quickened under Āeñāriōñ as the works of the government island drew labour, stone and starsteel from every province — Dārlinion and Ghisazma both reaching, within a generation, the scale of the capital itself. By RŌĀ 1017 every wall marked inviolate by ancient decree still stands, with far more built up around each one than any earlier age managed.

A Common Grammar#

Height carries rank as much as capacity in Vysoan building, at every scale it appears — the same drum-and-dome-or-spire grammar the government island wears at its largest (Maegysdārarziēri spires at one extreme, Gaomajenti drums at the other) simply repeats itself smaller everywhere else: a round or polygonal drum, capped by a dome for the gentler civic register or a spire for the more assertive one. Left alone, an ordinary building settles around eight to ten storeys (roughly forty metres), drum and cap together; wealthier city cores push the same shape to twenty or forty storeys without changing its grammar. Nothing beyond the government island itself is built to approach the thousand metres reserved for the Maegysdārarziēri alone.

The Vantage — Grand Strategy Toward the Wider Galaxy#

Set down under Āedāriōñ as the first drive neared working order, seven strategic threads, reckoned against a galaxy no Vysoan has yet seen and whatever peoples it may hold:

1. Waystation. Drydocks and cargo storage offered to whatever traffic the lanes beyond Vēzos come to carry, at rates no rival port will want to match. 2. Fleet for hire. Escort and security contracts, the Navy's hulls hired out to protect the convoys of others once there are others to protect. 3. Financial haven. The crown's vaults opened to outside depositors, backed by close on a thousand years without a default, and by the crown's own currency, Vēzqelde ("Gold of the Sun") — any purchase on Vysoan ground settles in Vēzqelde alone. 4. Knowledge hub. New archives and colleges, chartered to hold what no single world's library holds complete. 5. System colonization. Vēzperzyon grown from a foothold into a true colony, Taēsār and Merāeksys worked by extraction stations, Morghūl's modest station doubling as a quiet watch over the system's edge, refinery stations around Vermitos and Vagus. 6. Evangelization. The Covenant's missionaries riding whatever trade lanes open, absorbing compatible faiths for goodwill rather than converting by force. 7. A democratic face. Succession, marriage law, and the tradition of the gift stay strictly internal; the realm's voice abroad, the Jilēnys, is filled by election of the Gerialbar rather than royal appointment.

Where they stand (RŌĀ 1017). Of the seven, colonization (thread 5) has advanced furthest, being the only thread a single-system realm could pursue alone: Vēzperzyon holds a small but permanent colony; Taēsār, Merāeksys and the gas giants carry automaton-tended extraction and refinery stations with small crews; Morghūl's station keeps its watch. Vēzqelde (thread 3) is a digital currency in everyday use at home (see Coin and Revenue), though no outside depositor has yet come to test the vaults. The other threads stand ready rather than running. The waystation (thread 1) is so far the crown's own yards, where the first drive-fitted hulls are being built; the escorts (thread 2) wait on traffic that does not yet exist. The archives and colleges (thread 4) are chartered to admit foreign scholars of any people, should any be met, their certified copies to travel as gifts of state. The Covenant's missions (thread 6) are planned but unsent. The democratic face (thread 7) holds in form: the office of Jilēnys, elected by the Gerialbar, stands ready to speak for Vysos to the first people it meets.

The Witness of the Eye#

Of all five senses, Vysoans trust sight above the rest, and the habit runs through everything above: a king's legitimacy rests on the record and the statue chosen for how he'll be remembered, a building's rank is read from its height at a glance, and the Covenant's rarest gift comes to the Ūndissari as a vision seen rather than a voice heard. This is not love of beauty for its own sake but an instrument of proof — what fades from hearing or memory cannot be verified again, while what stands in stone or is entered in record can be checked by every generation after, which is much of why a people who leave nothing to be seen unsettle the realm more than any difference of blood or belief.

How the Realm Reckons a Stranger#

Reception turns on descent and record, not kind — the court asks of any newcomer, whether from the realm's own far shores or, as it now prepares to ask, from beyond Vēzos, whose line he is and what that line answers for, and has resolved to receive an envoy of standing, human or otherwise should the stars hold others, with the same courtesy any respected foreign dignitary gets. What stays closed to every newcomer alike, whatever their kind, is the bloodline itself: the corridor of thirty-eight kings, the Scions' own hereditary calling, the throne's own unbroken succession — a narrower exclusion than cruder prejudices practise, no less firmly kept for being narrow. The Covenant's habit of grading a foreign faith rather than demanding it be abandoned extends the same way to whatever a people believes, whatever they look like believing it, and settlers from beyond the realm's borders, of whatever people, are expected, over a generation or two, to become Vysoan rather than remain a colony planted inside Vysoan borders. Friction, where it persists, sits in habit more than law: a court fond of the rare and imported is practised at admiring the foreign as curiosity before it learns to meet it as colleague.

A people that keeps nothing lasting behind it — no monument, no archive, no traceable line — is read far less comfortably. The realm measures a people's having mattered by what survives of them in stone or record, and the Jorgūrēnti are sent out in part to gather into the Covenant's archives what an unlettered or nomadic people keeps only in memory, from old unease at impermanence rather than any wish to claim the credit — an unease the realm's own history justifies, so much of Valiērīa and its forty Zaldrāeksi families having passed in the Cataclysm into a silence the record can now only describe, never fill. Agrarian peoples read more gently than nomadic ones: rootedness tended across generations is a value the realm already practises at its own vast scale, while nomadism cuts against nearly everything the realm holds about staying and building being simply what a serious people does — tempered only by the same humility the throne shows any foreign method once proven, since a people who endure without a single wall to show for it have solved, by their own means, the very problem the realm has spent close on a thousand years solving by its own.

Coming to Vysos#

Vysos has yet to receive a visitor from beyond its own system, but its law already stands written for the day it does. A foreigner enters Vysos on one of two passes: a short entry pass, good for up to thirty Vysoan days, or a long-term pass, good for up to ninety. Either is approved on presentation of travel documents meeting the standards the realm sets. On arrival the visitor submits the address at which he will stay for the term of his visit and the intent of the visit, and the whole of it can be done digitally. Once within the realm, every law of the realm applies to him: Vysos keeps no separate law for Vysoans and for others.

A Vysoan is normally addressed by his first name; in a formal setting, by his family name with a polite honorific. A foreigner who wishes to speak with a Vysoan is expected to speak first. If a Vysoan answers a question with "Why do you ask?", the visitor should share his reasons, and can expect a much better answer once he has. Visitors whose own peoples habitually infer the intent behind another's questions are advised to refrain from doing so here: a Vysoan will not attempt to infer the meaning behind a visitor's question, since a question may have many purposes, and expects the same courtesy in return.

Dragons are still kept on Vysos, and visitors may see them. They are ridden as ceremonial mounts by the nobility.

Those Who Stay#

Foreigners who live in Vysos beyond a visit do so in one of four standings: holders of a work pass, the dependants of work pass holders, permanent residents, and the dependants of permanent residents. None of the four carries the franchise, which belongs to citizens alone. The Common Floor reaches each of them, deepening as a person's attachment to the realm deepens: no one lawfully resident in Vysos goes without healthcare or safety, whatever his standing.

A work pass is tied to its term and to the employer and role named on it. Its holder receives healthcare, safety and utilities, and chooses his own place of accommodation, the realm making its guides and resources for finding a home readily available to him. His dependants live in Vysos for as long as his pass runs; they share his healthcare, their children are schooled, and they may not take up work without a pass of their own. A work pass holder may apply for permanent residence after a qualifying period.

A permanent resident lives in Vysos without term and works without restriction. The Common Floor reaches him nearly in full — healthcare, housing, utilities, transport and education — with citizens given priority only where supply is limited. He may begin the recalibration that leads to naturalisation. His dependants share his standing for as long as he holds it, and children raised through Vysoan schooling come to naturalisation far more readily than adults, the formation they have received standing in the place of recalibration.

Two further standings stand apart from the four. A student enrolled in a Vysoan institution holds a student pass, which allows him to remain for the whole term of his study and for around two Vysoan years after it to find work, should he wish to. Because a student is not yet fully trained for work and still requires life's necessities, the student pass carries the Common Floor's subsidies and provisions, as the realm provides for its own young in formation. Students who find work pass on to a work pass, and from there may follow the road to permanent residence.

Those fleeing a crisis on their home world are to be given refugee status. They would be assessed, processed and housed as their needs require, in communities on one of the reserves Vysos stands ready to set aside, until the crisis at home resolves. Their children would be taught in special Vysoan schools set up for the purpose for as long as the need lasts.

Work for adult refugees remains a matter under deliberation, not from any wish to withhold it, but because work in Vysos is scarce and asks much of anyone not formed in the Vysoan method. The courses recommended to the realm are four, and need not exclude one another: work within the refugee communities themselves, in their administration, teaching, translation, mediation and the care of their own vulnerable; the crafts, since a people's own traditions of handwork are prized in Vysos and the realm stands ready to make a market for foreign craftsmanship; formation in the Vysoan method as a principal occupation, supported by a stipend, through which those who reach parity may pass on to a work pass; and preparation for return, planning and training for the rebuilding of their home world alongside Vysoan consultants, so that the eventual homecoming is ordered rather than a second displacement.

Permanent residence is open to a foreigner after around ten years of continuous residence. He must show good conduct and evidence of having assimilated: proficiency in Common Vysoan, the incorporation of Vysoan values into his own conduct, and completion of the recalibration curriculum. His application is weighed by a consultative panel of his neighbours, colleagues and supervisors, with independent magistrates sitting alongside them, and every member of the panel declares any interest he holds in the outcome.

A dependant of a work pass holder may apply for a work pass of his own while still holding his dependant's pass; all that is required is a letter from a corporation or registered Vysoan enterprise willing to hire him. A work pass holder may transfer directly to another employer, provided one will take him. A work pass ends when its holder's employment ends, and he is then given six Vysoan months to find new work. Permanent residence is not revoked unless its holder commits a serious crime or becomes a menace to society, meaning crimes that disrupt society and show him ill suited to life in Vysos.

Residents may bring family members from abroad to join them. Refugees may do the same once they themselves have been processed, a condition set not from any unwillingness but from caution. Should the crisis on a refugee people's home world not resolve, the realm looks to settle them more lastingly: on Vēzperzyon, or on an unclaimed world under Vysoan oversight. On such a world Vysos would provide the essentials, help raise its infrastructure swiftly, establish a provisional government, and guide the world toward membership of the commonwealth of worlds the realm envisages. Vysos has not yet faced a refugee crisis; these provisions stand ready against one.

A being of other physiology may naturalise as a citizen of Vysos, holding every right of citizenship save the vote.

Besides those displaced by a crisis, Vysos grants asylum to the individual fleeing persecution, provided he can bring evidence of it. Any foreigner whose pass or residence is refused or revoked may appeal the decision to the local arm of the judiciary for review.

Should sanctuary ever need to be given to those whom a greater power hunts — none has yet come seeking it — the realm stands ready to keep it apart from the state's own records: held off Vȳsōs itself, through bodies that would stand outside the Magistracies' record-keeping and answer to the Kardārys alone. The state would not falsify what it records; it would decline to know. A Magistracy answering that it holds no record of a person would be answering truly, and coming from a realm that keeps its records as meticulously as Vysos does, it would be meant to be believed.

Part III · Faith and Thought · Section 04 of 15

Doctrine & Religion

The Gift UndressedTwo Empires That Cannot Both Be RightThe Wound at the CataclysmThe Covenant's CustomsPrayer Through the SevenThe Oath of Office

What the Sidereal Covenant actually teaches, what it holds the gift to be, and the one rival claim and one old wound it has had to reckon with across the realm's history.

The Gift Undressed#

Read plainly, the Sidereal Covenant's oldest teachings on the gift are less a syncretic invention than a true account of the gifted, worn smooth by a thousand years of retelling. The seers' flame-visions are scrying, the gift's farthest sight practised by those born to it, and disciplined only as far as the Ūndissari have since learned to discipline it; the Corruption — already doctrinally widened to a metaphysical condition rather than a single being — is the bent in things that the gift, like every other power, can be turned to serve; and the Founder's line is held to carry the gift more surely than any other, attached to a bloodline rather than to a single life. The dragons read as fauna bonded through the gift, pairing for life and answering to blood before command, which recasts the Covenant's one truly unusual marriage law — sibling marriage, permitted only to houses of Valiērian descent — as a centuries-long breeding programme for concentrating that gift in a single line.

The gift has never broken the doctrine's habit of grading every faith it meets — it only handed that habit its widest test, which it passed by absorbing rather than by breaking. The river cults and hearth-gods of the old city states were graded exactly as the faiths of the Seven and of the flame once were when the Founder joined them: not rival truths, but the same truth met at a further remove. In the generations before the Solar Scions were made a standing institution, a common-born child found to carry the gift was preached as the Starshaper marking that child to carry the flame among the commons; since Kēlāeriōñ established the Scions, every gifted subject passes to the Order instead, a practice Valkarōz later codified. As the realm now enters the galaxy, the same habit stands ready for whatever faiths it meets there, each to be graded by how much of the good it has kept.

Two Empires That Cannot Both Be Right#

Every faith the Covenant has absorbed so far lacked a rival claim to being the light. Sȳndorīa breaks that pattern: its own antiquity, its tradition of god-emperors, and its teaching that its sacred kingship was older than Valiērīa itself made it a second realm with the same theological claim the Vēzgharyōñ have made for themselves. The collision resolves in the oldest terms the house has ever accepted an answer in: Vēzāeriōñ 's war against Sȳndorīa (RŌĀ 799–829), which absorbed its heartland of Qelendie and Sȳndoval, is read not as conquest alone but as trial by fire, the same test the Covenant applies to a single soul standing the Trial of Flame and Shadow — Sȳndorīa falls, no line survives to press the claim further, and the flame has testified.

The unmapped hemisphere on the world's far side poses a harder problem, since it is not a rival claim but a blank the doctrine has no tool for. It closes only late, and quietly: satellites carried aloft under Valkarys and kept in continuous service since RŌĀ 741 render the hemisphere mapped within years — mountain, coastline, and river system logged from orbit. What they find is a hemisphere of empty shore and wilderness, holding no people and no claim of its own. The house lets it be; no expedition is mounted in force, and no doctrine is drafted to grade what lives there.

The Wound at the Cataclysm#

Under this same reading, the Cataclysm that destroyed Valiērīa was not simply a geological catastrophe but a wound in the gift itself — the Zaldrāeksi of the forty families running their bond with dragon and earth past anything their own discipline governed, until the land answered. Dragons, themselves bonded through the gift, are exactly the wrong creatures to send into such a wound, and none went near the shattered Valiērian peninsula — not even Āelyxanthor 's own, on his three voyages back to Valiērīa — until Rāethor 's campaign finally cleansed the ruin, five centuries after the Founder's day.

That cleansing was also the first great labour of the house's own order of the gifted. Reclaiming what the shattered peninsula held required adepts who could walk into a corrupted place and return whole, minds unbent by what lingered there. Such adepts had grown up among the Ūndissari, the gifted seers of the flame, long before any king gave them a charter; Kēlāeriōñ made them a standing institution of the Crown, and Valkarōz later codified their rule, branches, dress and oath. What grew from that native root took its own name and structure: the Kardārōñe Qogrorāzma Vēzenkelarie, the Imperial Military Order of the Solar Scions — see The Solar Scions.

The Covenant's Customs#

Founded RŌĀ 52 under Āelyxanthor , merging the faith of Sētegqēlosiēr the Starshaper, the faith of the Seven, and beliefs gathered from disparate lesser creeds into a single Covenant identity, marked by a red seven-pointed star on a flaming border over a darkened steel field. Clergy run three tiers: the Eglābaros (Chief Illuminator, male only, head of the faith, under whose jurisdiction the Solar Scions are nominally held) over the Jehābaros/Jehābara (Illuminator of the Faithful, who sit together in conclave as the College of Jehābari) over the Sīvoktyr/Sīvokta (Priest/Priestess of the Seven, who perform rites and hear confession), robed alike in red, gold, and white worked with flame motifs and the Covenant's own roundel, richness rising with rank from the Sīvoktyr's plainer cloth to the Eglābaros's fullest, each keeping a standard vestment for ordinary duty beside a grander one for the high rites — the Eglābaros's own ceremonial dress, gold-crowned and roundel-set the length of it, pitched deliberately near the Kardārys's own idiom of gold and flame, red standing where his is black.

Marriage is monogamous by default, save for the sibling-marriage exception already noted, reserved to Valiērian-descended houses. Cremation is the preferred rite of burial — dragonfire specifically for House Vēzgharyōñ, held purest — with bodies lost at sea held in liturgical limbo until prayer brings them home. Household piety runs to dragon figures warding doors and a lamp kept lit overnight, its extinguishing before morning read as an ill omen.

Temple images hold one rule of likeness above all others. Sētegqēlosiēr, the Starshaper, is given a face the faithful can recognize and hold in memory, but he is never depicted alone. As he has only ever shown his will through the Seven, so he is shown only in their company. He stands at the heart of the star, armoured in gold beneath a white mantle, a circlet of gold on his brow and a halo of seven stars about it, a star held in his hands. About him the Seven are set in the order of the rainbow, parted by a white star of seven points, each bearing the sign of their office: Drējegros, the Warrior, in red; Vȳsēterys, the Smith, in orange; Jēdkeporys, the Father, in gold; Glaemunyñ, the Mother, in green; Arljēdryñ, the Maiden, in blue; Maegūryñ, the Crone, in indigo; and Morgharlax, the Stranger, in violet. Its essentials are fixed and repeated rather than left to any one artist's invention: the god at the heart of the white star and never alone, his halo of seven stars, and the Seven about him in the order of the rainbow, each with the sign of their office. So a subject who has seen one true image is held, in the Covenant's own reckoning, to have seen them all. Its fullest statement is the great window behind the high altar of the Barsīvōñ, the Hall of Seven Lights, a tall round-headed light some 17 metres across and 30 high, with the heavens above its rose and, below, the forge, the tree, and the sea from which the palace mount was raised. The clergy read the image according to their own division: to some, the Seven are the one light parted, as glass parts the sun; to others, they are seven lights set about their source. He is styled Ȳse Qēlosie Anarōvegliss, "His Sidereal Sublimity" (in address, Ēurar Qēlosie Anarōvegliss), one degree above the Kardārys's Imperial Majesty.

The Starshaper among the Seven — the Covenant's fixed likeness, as glassed in the great window of the Barsīvōñ

Within those essentials the lesser images may vary. The god may hold the finished star, as in the great window, or strike a star into being at an anvil, the Starshaper's name made literal; and the frame may suit its setting. Two smaller forms are most common: a square panel, kept in the homes of the devout, whose forging image is favoured by the Smith's guilds and in craftsmen's houses; and a wide panel, the rose set within an arcade, which stands above the altars of the smaller temples.

The Starshaper at the Anvil — the square panel of the household
The Starshaper among the Seven — the lesser window of the smaller temples

Five rites structure devotion: the Vigil of the Flames (a temple vigil from evening to small hours, with 7-night and 49-night purifying forms — the same vigil a subject facing a choice beyond his own power to settle is turned toward, its length scaled to the choice's own weight rather than told him by any fixed rule), Hearth Prayer (voluntary household evening devotion), the Absolution of the Sacred Flame (confession to a Sīvoktyr alone, its seal broken only on pain of the confessor's own Trial of Flame and Shadow), the Dawn Vigil (a kindled fire at sunrise), and Petitioning the Embers (a written plea burned in temple flame). A five-tier sin code, binding on all subjects and not Covenanters alone, ran as first written from a single Vigil of the Flames for lesser offences up through the Trial of Fire (adultery, apostasy, sexual deviancy, extinguishing a temple flame, or dishonouring the King) and the Trial of Flame and Shadow (blasphemy, or prophecy claimed without licence; invocable as a right by anyone accused with guilt in doubt) to outright drowning for the gravest offences — kinslaying, regicide, dragon-slaying, and dragon-binding by the gift without leave among them. Ēlyāegon reshaped that code at the Great Council (RŌĀ 380–390, held with the Eglābaros and the College of Jehābari): lèse-majesté was relaxed rather than repealed (constructive criticism now permitted, publicly insulting the King or hindering his duties still not); the adultery clauses were struck outright, enforcement having already lapsed for most of the realm's history, marital discord becoming a purely civil matter with the Covenant's own role narrowed to guidance and reconciliation and atonement made equal between the sexes; apostasy was struck as well, its own enforcement lapsed for generations, leaving it frowned upon but no longer unlawful; and the ban on falsely claiming visions was struck in turn, the Council holding a false seer better exposed by the Ūndissari's own scrutiny than by trial — a scrutiny that became the seers' sole lawful claim on prophecy when Valkarōz formalised it three centuries later. The Council marks the Covenant's own turn from an adjudicator to a counselor — its authority thereafter resting on influence and multi-generational trust rather than the law's own force. By RŌĀ 1017 what the Council left standing has itself receded further from ordinary use, supplanted under the Magistracy of Vettsīrdārdrīvo's administration by censure, fine, and loss of standing — though the old trials remain on the books and claimable as a right. Since the Solar Scions hold exclusive lawful claim to the use of the gift, the code's surviving ban on witchcraft now reads, in practice, as a ban on the gift's use outside the Order's sanction. The Council also gave the faith its own roundel, struck new for its own record — gules, a mullet of seven points argent, a ray Or issuant from between each of its points, within a bordure Or — shown wherever a temple, a Sīvoktyr's own seal, or a Covenant institution must be known at a glance, standing beside rather than replacing the ancient sigil of Āelyxanthor 's own founding proclamation.

Prayer Through the Seven#

The Covenant does not teach that the Starshaper desires prayer for its own sake. Its rites exist for the one who keeps them: chiefly for discernment, as the Vigil of the Flames already is, and beyond that to bring the faithful into the frame of mind an act demands before it is undertaken. A Vysoan prays to prepare, settling resolve and fixing intention before the deed; to examine his own conduct against the Covenant's teaching; to find steadiness in grief or suffering, not so that the suffering will be lifted, but so that it may be rightly borne; and, in the rites kept together, to remember and to bind the faithful to one another. What the Covenant does not countenance is prayer as tribute, appeasement, or bargain: the Starshaper is not bought, and no rite is kept to purchase his favour or turn aside his displeasure.

Prayers are accordingly addressed to whichever of the Seven embodies the virtue the moment calls for: to Jēdkeporys, the Father, for right judgment and authority justly used, before judging, governing, or making law; to Glaemunyñ, the Mother, for comfort, and for mercy both received and given, in grief or sickness and before forgiving; to Arljēdryñ, the Maiden, for hope and renewal, at new undertakings, at betrothal, or after failure; to Maegūryñ, the Crone, for wisdom and good counsel, in study and in hard decisions; to Morgharlax, the Stranger, for discernment and a clear conscience, in self-examination and at the approach of death; to Drējegros, the Warrior, for courage and the strength to choose right, before battle, trial, or temptation; and to Vȳsēterys, the Smith, for diligence, skill, and endurance, before labour and the work of making.

Nor does the Covenant promise miracles. The Starshaper, it teaches, grants none; he provides instead the avenues by which a creature may achieve them for itself. An answered prayer is therefore one that changes the one who prays — the soldier given courage to fight rightly rather than a promise of victory, the mourner given strength to bear a loss rather than the return of the dead — and the faith holds no prayer disproven by misfortune, since none was ever offered to prevent it.

The Oath of Office#

Every office of real weight is entered the same way, sworn upon the Covenant with a lit flame and the right hand set on the Udirēr Jaehose, "The Word of God" — the Covenant's own holy book, called in everyday speech simply the Udirēr, "the Word" — the moment the realm's doctrine of charge and obligation is understood to take hold from.
