The realm's ethical doctrine proper, drawn together from where it had grown up scattered across dynastic custom, statecraft, the Covenant's own teaching, and the Solar Scions' theology alike. The Covenant has never been the sole wellspring of Vysoan judgment — a body of intellectual rigor distinct from any temple flame has reasoned through the realm's hardest questions for a thousand years alongside it.

A Practice the Realm Outgrew#

Slavery was struck from Vysoan law centuries past, argued since chiefly on grounds of competence rather than conscience: a subject who labors from fear alone bears no love for the work, aspires to no legacy the realm could credit, and reliably produces work merely adequate — anathema to a realm that measures a life by the legacy built across it. A people found still practicing slavery, should the realm meet one among the stars, would be read as backward on this reasoning alone, not chiefly for the cruelty but for the plain inefficiency of building an economy atop labor that can never be more than adequate.

The Task, Not the Hour#

Free labour is ordered on the same reasoning that abolished slavery. The measure is the greatest gain for the least labour, and the unit is the task and the objective, not the hour. A subject is charged with an allocated responsibility and judged by whether it is discharged. Whoever finishes sooner keeps the rest of his time for leisure, not for more work. Pay by time served is held an inefficiency, kept only where an office demands presence, and even then the demand is that someone be present when needed, not that every hand be held in place. Processes are built, wherever they can be, to run without a body standing over them. Mundane, unsophisticated labour is treated as a cost to be designed down and automated, so that subjects are freed for work that wants judgment and skill. No subject is meant to stay at a task for long stretches without relief: work and leisure run with some flexibility between them, since a rested mind gives better work than an exhausted one.

A Kindness Freely Given#

Charity sits deliberately outside the realm's doctrine of charge and office: an office creates an obligation to act, but no comparable obligation attaches to simple kindness. Generosity toward the needy is called for, commended, and woven through the Covenant's own teaching at every rank — but the moment it is made a command rather than left a choice, the realm holds it has stopped being charity in anything but name, since an act performed under duress answers to the pressure rather than to the giver's own will. A subject is free to withhold a kindness without breaking any law the realm keeps, whatever quiet ledger the realm's own opinion keeps instead.

The Root Before the Remedy#

Charity answers a need for a night, not its return the next morning, and no house commands wealth enough to feed every mouth the realm holds — a truth the Covenant states plainly rather than treats as an embarrassment to its own teaching on kindness. Where want recurs rather than merely occurs, the Covenant's actual answer has never rested on any single house's freely given generosity: it rests on law passed at every tier of government, on welfare measures administered to the many rather than the one, and on the teaching of a trade, so a subject fed today need not be fed again tomorrow by anyone's charity at all. A recurring want is read as a failure of governance rather than a shortfall of individual generosity, and a Vysoan solution is judged chiefly by whether it lifts the many at once rather than the one case standing before it.

No Envy Between Roles, Care After Service#

No ethical distinction is drawn between the sexes in duty to office or in inheritance; the difference the realm recognizes lies only in the roles a life more commonly settles into, not in the weight the Covenant assigns them — an office-holder and a household-keeper are read as fulfilling functions the realm holds equally vital, owing each other no envy for the difference in scope. The Covenant carves one exception from that equality, and names it as such rather than leaving it to be found: the throne itself, and the Eglābaros's chair beside it. Neither is reckoned an office the realm created, to be apportioned by the realm's own ethic, but a charge the Covenant holds the Starshaper himself to have set — the throne passing down the Founder's line by the agnatic preference it has kept since its founding — sons before daughters, a daughter's son inheriting only when no male-line heir remains, as Auriōñ did — and the Eglābaros's chair held a man's since Āelyxanthor first joined the faiths into one — and what the realm did not make, the Covenant holds, the realm's ethic has no standing to remake. Everywhere beneath those two seats, estate and office pass without regard to sex. Where the realm's own service has left a subject unable to provide for himself, a veteran maimed in the Crown's wars foremost among them, the same systemic answer given for chronic want extends to him as a matter of course: care and support administered through law rather than left to wait on any house's charity, since a want the realm's own service created is a want the realm owes itself to answer.

The Realm's Magnificence#

At the root of Vysoan civic life lies a single conviction, taught from the first years of Personal Formation: I work for the realm's magnificence, for my magnificence is the realm's, and the realm's magnificence is mine. Where the Common Floor has removed want as a reason to labour, it supplies the reason that remains. Every Vysoan, whatever door he passed through, adds to the same splendour and shares in it alike, the hand that keeps a line honest no less than the mind that decides. The bargain runs both ways and is kept on both sides: what a Vysoan gives is held in common, and the realm returns it in the halls, the libraries and the ceremonies open to all, and in the floor that sustains every citizen.

It is for this reason that the individual is restrained and the realm is magnificent. Personal display adds nothing to a realm where fine things are common and a role is never a rank, and pride, which might otherwise be spent on outshining one's neighbour, is spent instead on the common work. Even the Kardārys's splendour is the throne's, not the man's: in the vestments he dresses as the realm, not as himself.

Three qualifications keep the conviction from its own corruption. First, the realm's magnificence is not its own end: the realm is splendid because it is a rightly ordered work within the Starshaper's design, and its splendour answers to that design rather than to itself. Second, since every failure diminishes what all hold in common, to expose a failure and correct it is service to the realm's magnificence, never disloyalty to it; the review that finds a fault honours the realm more than the silence that would hide it. Third, the realm's magnificence is a standard to be served, not a rank to be held over others: it gives a Vysoan cause to work, never cause to look down on those outside it, and pride that turns to contempt for other peoples is counted a diminishment of the very splendour it claims.

The Raising of an Heir#

No regency has ever yet been called upon in the house's whole record — read less as fortune than as the natural consequence of a family this deep in cadet branches, which has never yet wanted for a member of good enough bearing to hold the office — nor has the house ever had cause to set an heir aside; prevailing thought holds the Starshaper himself to have agency in an heir's forming, so whatever fault a prince is born or grows carrying is read as intended toward some purpose the realm has not yet been shown. Fostering, by contrast, is settled and active among the noble houses — a son or daughter sent to be raised some years under another house's roof to build goodwill and personal bond, and, by the realm's own reckoning of how a mind is formed, to transfer knowledge and mentality besides, which is why the choice of foster house is weighed with real seriousness. Adoption keeps no such standing: it is no practice of the nobility or the imperial family at all, held anathema to be taken into a house one was not born to, a reluctance sharpened past ordinary aristocratic suspicion of an unproven line by the bloodline's own gift. Deliberate breeding for the gift has had no need to continue in the old sibling-marriage sense for centuries, the same end now served indirectly through the sheer breadth of cadet houses the blood has thrown off — a match with any cadet branch, or any subject of proven descent from Āelyxanthor , sufficing for the imperial house. Among the wider nobility, marriage requirements vary house to house, but where the imperial and cadet lines are not directly concerned, compatibility and a shared vision for the house's future weigh more heavily than love is generally permitted to; consent of both parties is asked as a matter of course regardless, a marriage entered without it held already failing, whatever calculation went into arranging it. A cadet house's own ambition toward greater standing troubles no one so long as it stays lawful, the throne asking its branches only to seek more of it honestly — though the throne keeps an equal right to interfere wherever it judges the seeking has strayed.

The Charge and the Unbidden Hand#

One piece of the Covenant's moral teaching outlived the law it once enforced: a doctrine holding that a subject invested with charge over some working of consequence — a magistrate, a ship's officer, a watchman set to a mechanism whose failure could cost lives — has already accepted the burden of acting should that charge turn dangerous, and that standing by while positioned to prevent a graver harm is read as a failure of the office itself, no cleaner than acting wrongly would have been, since a role left unfilled at the moment it matters is filled by no one. A stranger who holds no such charge is measured differently — to ask an unbidden hand to become, of its own motion, the instrument of a harm it was never charged with weighing is to ask it to manufacture what the realm never gave it leave to decide, and the Covenant holds a life taken by a hand with no charge apart from a duty discharged by a hand that held one. An act of such weight must be one the realm's records can hold and explain afterward — a hand with no charge to point to leaves nothing for the record to point to but the taking itself.

The Reckoning of the Many#

Where two duties collide, precedence goes to whichever answers the larger body of those it touches — a subject torn between claims asks first what most serves his own community, then what most serves Vysos entire, and follows whichever answer points further outward. Every office likewise answers to a code beyond its holder's own judgment: an officer who witnesses a superior order a clear wrong is obliged to refuse it and report the matter, but where the order is merely suspected of wrong rather than shown to be so, obedience holds instead, and the concern is filed for later review.

The Vicegerent's Judgment#

The Great Council's reform did not touch the Crown's own separate authority to judge and to punish. As Jentys Pāsābarie, Commander of the Faithful, and as the Founder's heir in his own generation, the Kardārys holds judgment of crime and the administration of justice — capital judgment included — as the throne's own prerogative rather than the Covenant's. The five-tier code's harshest penalties were narrowed in practice rather than struck, and though censure, fine, and loss of standing now answer most transgressions, the gravest matters — kinslaying, regicide, and their like — remain the King's to judge in the last resort, answering to his own vicegerency rather than to any institutional authority the Covenant retained. He observes no rite before pronouncing such a sentence — he speaks it in his own name, that name already carrying the Starshaper's own authority into the word. Nor does the Covenant's teaching that no creature is faultless exempt the man who wears the crown. The Kardārys strives as every creature strives, and passes before Morgharlax, the Stranger, at his death as every soul does; what the Covenant holds preserved from error is the office, not the man — the judgments he renders as vicegerent, in the Starshaper's name, kept by the Starshaper's providence from leading the realm astray, whatever faults the man himself must answer for.

Mitigation, the Flame, and Reachable Mercy#

A criminal's sentencing may be mitigated where his own formative circumstances are shown to have been truly deficient — a mind poorly formed bearing less weight than one well formed and still gone wrong — though the realm leans on this mercy only as a last resort, since schooling grounds every child in the Covenant from the earliest years regardless of household, and the wider community is expected to stand as a second net beneath that first one. A child short of his majority is held culpable all the same, though the penalty he answers to is lessened for the formation he has not yet finished receiving, and such a case is read as cause to examine the household or school that let it go wanting. Death by one's own hand is forbidden absolutely and without exception: a subject's flame of life is the Starshaper's own to give, and his alone to decide when it is extinguished. Mercy shown to another beyond hope of relief is sanctioned only where circumstance leaves genuinely no other mercy reachable — deep wilderness with no medical care within any reach, say — and never where an alternative, however distant or costly, still stands.

A Faculty Surrendered#

The Covenant admonishes intoxication without forbidding it outright, and Vysoan ethics beyond the Covenant's own teaching reaches the same caution unprompted: a being who drinks, smokes, or otherwise clouds himself past command of his own faculties has, for that span, surrendered by his own hand the very mind the realm's law guards so carefully against a stranger's tampering. The intoxicant itself carries no prohibition — wine, smoke, and their like are no transgression merely for being taken, and a being who partakes in moderation, his own command still his to keep, has done nothing the Covenant finds fault with; what is admonished is the excess that spends that command away. The Covenant counsels against it most sternly where the surrender is sought for enjoyment's own sake rather than any weightier cause — a mind let loose from its own command in pursuit of pleasure alone is spending something dearer than the moment it buys, and imprudence, not sin, is the harshest word the Covenant keeps in reserve for the ordinary case of it.

A Stake Not Made a Habit#

Gambling, like intoxication, is admonished rather than forbidden and judged by the same measure: an occasional wager among friends for sport's own sake, hazarding little and meant only to sharpen an evening's pleasure, troubles no law and draws no particular censure. What the Covenant counsels against is the habit rather than the act — a subject who returns to the wager again and again, until laying it has become routine rather than occasion, is read as a subject who has let chance take a seat at his table it was never owed. The wisest course is to refrain from the practice altogether, not because the occasional wager is itself a fault, but because the line between an evening's diversion and a settled habit is more easily crossed than recrossed.

A Mind Kept Level#

Just as a mind given away to drink is admonished, both the Covenant and Vysoan ethics beyond it hold a mind given away to passion answerable to the same caution: emotional excess is admonished, and deciding anything of real weight in its grip is a fault of the same family as deciding it drunk. Custom counsels a calm disposition before any choice of consequence — not because feeling itself is a fault, but because a decision reached in anger, grief, or any passion running high is reached without the deliberation every grave choice is owed. To act emotionally is to act rashly, and a rash subject opens himself to error he would not otherwise have made.

Wrong Answered, and Left to Conscience#

A wrong between subjects scales in its response to the harm actually done: the Magistracy of Vettsīrdārdrīvo favors arbitration and mediation where the matter allows it, a subject may pursue the courts if he prefers, and a wrong done against a person is that person's alone to forgive, restitution paid to the one wronged rather than to the realm in his name. An ordinary lie, short of any gift worked to alter another's mind, answers to no law at all — the Covenant leaves it to conscience, holding a lie's discovery to already be its own consequence.

A Fool's Sacrifice, No Second Judgment#

Whether a sacrifice for some larger cause is honored or pitied turns entirely on the cause: worth the cost, it is honored; unworthy, it is read as a fool's act rather than a martyr's. And a subject who has taken a life in the lawful course of duty — soldier or the Crown's own officer alike — owes the realm no formal absolution after, though he may seek a Sīvoktyr's counsel if he wishes it; the deciding was never his alone to make.

Doctrine and the Gift's Limits#

Induction is asked of every gifted Vysoan as a mutual obligation rather than a mere calling — an untrained gift left to a family without the means to guide it is read as a danger left standing — and the Order does not ask an inductee to leave his family behind, adding itself to what already holds him rather than replacing it. A vision received by an Ūndissaros is reckoned already fixed to come, and the Order holds it fruitless to act for or against one, since acting against a dark vision leaves no way of ever knowing afterward whether the acting was what brought it to pass.

Bending another mind by telepathy — overriding its will rather than merely reading it — is outlawed and held a violation as much physical as mental, and the Order does not hold every quarrel resolvable by peaceable means; where words fail, fighting a quarrel out honestly is no dishonor. The gift's lawful reach is fourfold — telekinesis, telepathy, astral projection and scrying — and within the Order's sanction each is simple use of a gift the Starshaper granted, a fault to leave idle rather than a suspect act. Reading a mind to ascertain truth is held a just use of the same gift — though never trusted to one interrogator alone, every such finding checked and corroborated against another's independently obtained. Tales of the gifted mending a failing body by the gift alone are kept as legend and nothing more: the Order claims no such power, and the realm entrusts the sick to its physicians.

A Tool Weighed, Not Wielded Lightly#

War itself is treated as a tool of policy like any other, no more inherently dishonorable than a treaty, and reckoned by the same cold calculation the Covenant applies to a civilization's worth — justified only where benefit to the Vysoan populace is calculated to outweigh the fighting's cost, or where the realm's own defense against aggression leaves no calculation to make. The standing ban on bending a mind by the gift holds exactly as firmly on a battlefield as anywhere else, war being no exception the Covenant has ever carved out, and an enemy's resort to dishonorable means excuses a Vysoan nothing should he stoop to answer in kind. No rite precedes a declaration of war, unlike a capital sentence — war is reckoned by calculation rather than ceremony.

A Mind of Its Own#

The realm cannot yet grow a body whole, but its doctrine has already settled what such a body would be. A body cloned whole, rather than merely repaired in part, would form its own mind from the moment it began forming memory at all — its thoughts and cognition its own rather than any continuation of the mind its flesh was patterned after, so two witnesses sharing an identical vessel would remain, in the Covenant's own reckoning, two witnesses. A full clone would be reckoned a person of its own from the moment its own mind began. What marks that mind apart from an automaton's is the operation rather than the flesh: a living mind requires no charging and answers to no program, forming its own memory and arriving at its own thought by no process any engineer wrote in advance, where an automaton's mind, however sophisticated its behavior, remains programmed rather than self-arising. This distinction carries no license with it — cruelty toward an automaton is regarded, whatever its legal standing, as crude and uncivilized conduct unbecoming a subject of the realm. No degree of apparent sophistication moves this line: however convincingly an automaton's learning may one day come to imitate independent thought, what sits at its core remains unchanged, reprogrammable and its memory wipeable in a way no living mind has ever been shown to be — the realm does not ask an automaton's outward behavior to settle what its own architecture has already settled.

Autonomous Personhood#

The thinking machines the realm has built since Vēzāerys are rudimentary things, set to simple processes, and none has yet come near the question this doctrine answers; the doctrine is written for the machines the realm expects to build. Most automata are programmed minds without standing, as the realm's ethics hold. An automaton of sufficient personality and agency, however, may one day be held to have Autonomous Personhood, a category distinct from Organic Personhood, which leaves untouched the line already drawn between a living mind and an automaton's: no automaton becomes as a living creature is, though some may become persons of their own kind. The line is the demonstrated ability to act rightly above and beyond its original programming: the same first step out of the created-being mentality that the Covenant hopes for in every creature. The finer points are a matter for the Covenant and its clergy, who debate them at length.

The possibility would be slight in automata not engineered for significant personality, and greater in those designed for sophisticated tasks. Whether an automaton had crossed the line would be judged by a panel: officials of the government, a member of the clergy, and, most critically, those with whom the automaton deals each day. Those who deal with it would give their evidence, and any interest they hold in the outcome, as an owner's in his property, would be declared, so that no such interest decides the case alone.

An Autonomous Person would be served as a client in its own right. To move its mind into a new body would continue a person, and would require its consent; to wipe it would be a grave wrong; and whether it may be copied, which would make a second being, awaits the clergy's judgement.

The Will Left Free#

The Covenant holds that Sētegqēlosiēr, the Starshaper, authors each creature's spirit and its inclinations, and makes every one of them for a purpose of his own intending — but the will that acts upon those inclinations he leaves to the creature itself. Not every creature reaches the purpose it was made for, and the Covenant does not read that shortfall as a flaw in the making: it is the cost of a will that is truly a creature's own. Nor does the Order's teaching that a vision is fixed to come unsettle that freedom. The Starshaper sees what each creature will freely choose, and an Ūndissaros receives a glimpse of that seeing; but to see a choice is not to cause it, any more than a witness to a deed is its author. A vision is fixed because the choice it shows will be freely made, not made because the vision fixed it.

Corruption and the Choosing#

Every creature, the Covenant teaches, is made to desire the good. What bends that desire is not its making but a corruption lingering in the world, which turns intention and deed alike astray, and from that corruption comes the suffering the faithful see on every side. The choice it sets before each soul is the whole of the Covenant's moral drama: to yield to the corruption, or to heed the Starshaper's teaching — what he has found, across the long work of making, to be right and workable. This is what the Covenant names the Corruption — not a rival god, nor any being set against the Starshaper as an equal, but the name for that same lingering bent in things, which the older liturgy spoke of as though it were a person. The night the Scion's Oath bids banished is this Corruption, and the gift turned to ill, as the Covenant's own teaching on the gifted already holds, is its working in those who yield to it.

Mercy to the Striving#

The Starshaper is not without mercy, and the Covenant is plain about where that mercy falls: not upon the faultless, of whom it holds there are none, but upon those who strive to better themselves. A soul is weighed by the direction it walks rather than by whether it has yet arrived.

That mercy is accorded according to a creature's incapacities. Infants who die young are deemed innocent, and those who break beneath a suffering they could not bear are not condemned.

The Law Written Into Things#

The Starshaper's teaching rests on natural law — law written into the nature of things rather than handed down to one people alone — and the Covenant draws two consequences from it. The first concerns the untaught: never having been taught the Covenant is a mitigating condition when a soul is weighed, but it can mitigate only so far, since it would be highly irregular for any creature to be formed in a society holding no semblance of that law at all. The second concerns other faiths: as ultimate creator even of the variant faiths found across his world, the Starshaper has left in each of them at least an echo of what is good, if not a portion of what is known to be good. It is on this ground that the Covenant grades every faith it meets, measuring how much of the good each has kept, rather than condemning any of them wholesale.

Decay and Its Season#

The Covenant does not count decay among the Starshaper's enemies. Decay, it teaches, holds a purpose of its own in his design: to bring to an end those things whose time has passed. To name decay an enemy would be to claim that some part of nature lies beyond the Starshaper's power, and that claim the Covenant will not make. The enemy it names instead is disorder, chaos, and rebellion against the natural law. None of this asks the faithful to welcome the decay of their own works: creatures strive, and rightly, that what they make should not decay, refining their works continually toward that end. Yet the Covenant holds that decay remains a natural part of life, and that it has its role.

Made to Be Acted Upon#

The soul the Starshaper forms is never malformed, and the Covenant teaches that he did not intend his creations to remain incapable. It is just and right for a creature to make itself capable, and good to do so by artificial means; more than that, it is the Starshaper's design that his creations should. He expects them to use the knowledge and sciences made known to them to improve their lives, and the Covenant counts as misguided any notion that a purity of nature must be preserved against such improvement. The world was made to be acted upon, and it would be a disservice to its maker to leave it untouched.

The How and the Why#

The Covenant teaches that to contemplate how the world was made is as spiritual as to contemplate why it was made. Study of the stars, of matter or of the living body is holy work no less than meditation on the Starshaper's purpose, for both read the same design, and neither stands above the other. In the Covenant's own words, the why begot the how, and the how, the why.

The Stranger, at the Foot of the Star#

Of the Seven, the Covenant portrays Morgharlax, the Stranger, as androgynous, neither man nor woman, and gives decay into the Stranger's governance: decay is the Stranger's own domain, ruled as a sovereign rules a realm. Where the Seven are arranged as the points of the Covenant's seven-pointed star, the Stranger stands at its foot: the natural end of what Arljēdryñ, the Maiden, renews and what Vȳsēterys, the Smith, makes.

The Soul After Death#

The Covenant teaches that at death every soul passes before Morgharlax, the Stranger, and is judged. Those who have lived virtuously are rewarded; those who erred are corrected. A soul that has been rewarded, or one whose correction is done, may choose to remain in the afterlife, and no lesser honour attaches to that choice: a soul that has borne a harder life than others is served well by a season of rest.

A soul that has not yet reached its end is given the chance to return to life, and this the clergy hold not as speculation but as revelation, made known to them through a series of visions from the Starshaper. A returning soul comes back after its time in the afterlife with its memories wiped, yet not unchanged: its disposition, and its capacity for understanding, remain with it. In this the Covenant finds the reason that some appear more able to understand than others.

Souls that refuse correction are neither returned nor dissolved. They are held back in the Stranger's domain, in a state of limbo — unable to return, yet not undone — and there they are contained until such time as the Starshaper decides otherwise.

What the Clergy Ask in Private#

Two further teachings circulate among the Covenant's clergy as speculation, never as settled doctrine. The first holds that the present order of creation is only the latest of several, the earlier ones malformed, and that the Starshaper permits their remnants to linger because no creature can know what is good without also knowing what is not — so that the corruption bending the will is, on this reading, nothing other than those remnants. The second holds that the Starshaper's omniscience is functional rather than proven absolute: complete over everything his creatures could ever test, so that to them, for all intents and purposes, he is all-knowing. Neither has been ratified, and the clergy at large keep to the plainer teaching: that the evil in the world is caused by those who do not heed the Starshaper's wisdom and walk toward the path of right.

The Seven, and the Question Behind Them#

The Covenant's clergy hold one thing about the Seven with certainty: that the Starshaper has only ever conveyed his will, or shown it, through them — Jēdkeporys, the Father; Glaemunyñ, the Mother; Arljēdryñ, the Maiden; Maegūryñ, the Crone; Morgharlax, the Stranger; Drējegros, the Warrior; and Vȳsēterys, the Smith — the names the faithful know them by. Every rite and every devotion of the Covenant is accordingly offered through the Seven, since that is the only way the Starshaper has ever made himself known, and the clergy keep to it. That the Seven are his aspects is not in dispute; what an aspect truly is, is. One body of opinion holds them to be his very faces, the Starshaper himself seen from seven sides. Another holds them to be servants so wholly given over to his will that his will is seen through them alone. The question has never been settled, opinions among the clergy still differ, and the worship of the Seven has never waited on its answer.

The Thought of God#

The Covenant's catechism teaches of the Jaehotāsīr, a name meaning approximately "Thought of God": the spiritual being at the top of the cosmological order, just below the Starshaper. The Jaehotāsīr is begotten, not made, formed from the very thought of the Starshaper. It is the first being to hear his thoughts, and the foremost aide in his work of creation, assisting him in conceptualisation, hypothesis and possibility.

It is through the Jaehotāsīr that the Starshaper communes with the spiritual beings of the cosmological order and conveys his designs to them. Its will, the catechism holds, both exists and does not: it is not a separate being so much as a will that is part of the Starshaper's own, and yet not.

The Breath of God#

Beside the Jaehotāsīr, at parity with it but different in function, the catechism places the Jaehēlēpēl, a name meaning "the Breath Giver of God" or "the Animator of God." Where the Jaehotāsīr faces inward and upward, toward the Starshaper and his heavens, the Jaehēlēpēl faces outward into creation: it is the Starshaper's presence within his works.

The Jaehēlēpēl animates the living. It writes the natural law into the nature of things, which is why no society is ever wholly without it; it quickens conscience and discernment; and it leaves in every people at least an echo of the good. The Jaehotāsīr, the catechism teaches, is the Starshaper's thought received; the Jaehēlēpēl is his life given.

Three in Commune#

The catechism teaches that the Jaehotāsīr and the Jaehēlēpēl are not creatures set beneath the Starshaper but the Starshaper himself: one being in three, each present at once and each in total commune with the others. That they stand "just below" him names the order in which they come forth, not any lesser nature.

The Jaehēlēpēl is the substance of the thought that passes between the Starshaper and the Jaehotāsīr, emanating from them both outward. It has been since the beginning, for the Starshaper has always thought, and so the Breath has always been. It authors life's first spark, permeates creation, and sustains it in its essence, as the Orderers sustain its order. Because the Breath fills all things, the Ēlvesēli may work through it as a medium, and it is by this means that visions are sent: the charge of the Ēlvesēli, empowered by the Jaehēlēpēl.

Vysoans in general commonly go further and hold the Breath to be the wellspring of the gift itself: that what the gifted draw upon when they move a thing unseen, hear another's thought, walk abroad outside the body or scry what is to come is none other than the Jaehēlēpēl moving through them. It is a common interpretation among Vysoans at large, not a teaching of the catechism.

The Crown & Government

What Every Title MeansThe Nineteen ChairsThe Five Governances — From Township to Throne

The throne's own names and style, the nineteen chairs that administer the realm in its name, and the five tiers of government beneath them are covered together here, since scarcely one of the three can be explained cleanly without the other two.

What Every Title Means#

By RŌĀ 1017 the state carries two names for two occasions: Karadēmysēr Unavȳsōse — the Sublime Throne of All-Vysos — the full, formal name reserved for treaty and charter; and Dēmysēr Vȳsōse, the Vysoan Throne, worn day to day. The King's own style accreted clause by clause over some nine hundred years, no reign ever retiring what an earlier one claimed. Baeriōñ the Black, bringing the neighbouring city states to heel, claimed the first clause, Zirȳs Ñellenkaperzys; Auriōñ the Golden added Jentys Pāsābarie and Rāelagonēr Nāmorghūlperzyse in a single reign; Dārys (King) remained the plain royal word until Ēlyāegon the Enlightened added Kardārys (Great King) alongside it; Vēzāeriōñ the Magnificent became the first Dārysdāri (King of Kings) after his final war against Sȳndorīa; Vēzāeriōñ the Stargazer added Karāeksys Unavȳsōsii the reign the realm first set foot upon the Moon; and Āeñāriōñ claimed the newest clauses together, the threefold Trēsyvēzos (Son of the Sun), Gīmēperzys Nūmāzmēre (Beacon of Truth) and Zaldrīzēr Dorāzmēre (the Dragon of the Void), the same reign the colony and the system's stations were gathered under one Vȳse and the government island raised.

In full the style now runs Kardārys [name], Trēsyvēzos, Gīmēperzys Nūmāzmēre, Zaldrīzēr Dorāzmēre, Zirȳs Ñellenkaperzys, Dārysdāri, Jentys Pāsābarie, Rāelagonēr Nāmorghūlperzyse, Karāeksys Unavȳsōsii — spoken in order of precedence rather than of accretion. Five of its nine clauses speak to temporal rule, four to the Sidereal Covenant the throne has never let go of defending.

The Threefold Devotion

High Vysoan — solemn occasions:
Trēsyvēzos amīlōs. Gīmēperzys Nūmāzmēre ūbremōs. Zaldrīzēr Dorāzmēre jemīlōs.

Common Vysoan — mass public occasions:
Son of the Sun, guide us. Beacon of Truth, teach us. Dragon of the Void, protect us.

Beneath the throne, the Dēmōndosēr — the First Minister — heads government day to day. Cabinet posts carry the title Maegysdār (Wise Leader, nearer magister than minister in sense). The office of Jilēnys (Sent Voice), the realm's Envoy, stands ready to speak for Vysos to whatever peoples the stars may hold, though none has yet been met; its holder is elected by the Gerialbar, the realm's legislature, which sits as two houses: the Qupteōrion (Common Hall) below, and above it the Āeksiōrion, the upper house the nobility elects from its own number (see The Peerage).

The Nineteen Chairs#

The Qrogorjentys — Kardārōñe Qrogorjentys in full style — numbers nineteen as of RŌĀ 1017: the Kardārys, who chairs it in his own right; the Dēmōndosēr, who assists him and chairs in his absence; fifteen Maegysdāri, each answerable for one Magistracy; and two Gaomajenti, who answer instead for the throne's eyes and ears, upon Vȳsōs and beyond it both.

The Five Governances — From Township to Throne#

Government below the Nineteen Chairs runs in five nested tiers, largest to smallest — Giezverde (system-wide), Vȳse (regional), Rōvoktione (large city), Oktione (city), Naenitone (township) — each administered by its own Qrogorjentys paired with its own Gerialbar, mirroring the structure above it (a Naenitone's own Qrogorjentys alone excludes agency and defence/galactic-affairs seats). The structure grew organically, from Āelyxanthor 's single founding city through Vēzāeriōñ 's realm-wide formalization to Vēzāerys 's first Vȳse-tier governance, and was carried off-world when Vēzāerys planted the colony upon Vēzperzyon; by RŌĀ 1017 it comprises one Giezverde, seven Vȳse — one for each of the six continents of Vȳsōs (North and South Ēlythoros counted as one), and a seventh for Vēzperzyon, whose own Vȳse Jenaejot also answers for the extraction stations scattered across the system's other bodies — and fifteen Rōvoktioni, Zobrezos foremost among them.

Suffrage follows Ēlyrōz 's reform: any Maegystīrys holder — a Maegysombāzmion graduate — of 25 years or older may vote or stand for office; parties and factions are illegal, and campaigns are self-funded. The narrowness is deliberate rather than an oversight. Of the three tertiary doors, the Maegysombāzmion alone teaches the whole reckoning a vote demands — what, why, who, where, and when — where the Guildhall stops short of where and when, and the Trade Academy at how; to choose who governs, and to stand for governing, is itself the act of decision the Maegysombāzmion exists to train. Nor is the franchise read as a ranking of worth: the realm holds a position to be a role it needs filled rather than proof of its holder's standing against anyone else's, and the vote is reckoned a role of exactly that kind. Its door is never shut — a Botȳsgūrēñion leaver of the requisite aptitude may enter a Maegysombāzmion in an Otāgūrēñion graduate's stead, and a working life that runs to seventy leaves room to take that door later, as mid-life retraining already makes ordinary. The Iderlēnos ("Chosen Voice") career ladder begins at a Naenitone's own Gerialbar, paid a state wage. Selection above that first rung runs two distinct tracks: a Jovertys (Governor) is elected by the Gerialbar of the jurisdiction he will govern, drawn from candidates one tier higher — up to a Vȳse's own Gerialbar electing its Jovertys from the Giezverde's own Iderlēnos — with the Dēmōndosēr alone standing outside this ladder, appointed directly by the Kardārys from the Giezverde Āeksiōrion's nobles. A Maegysdār is instead appointed by that tier's own Jovertys from civil servants due for promotion, confirmed by the Gerialbar of the Jovertys's level; at the Giezverde's own tier the ladder forks, since most of the fifteen national Maegysdāri are drawn from the realm's highest-ranking civil servants already serving at that rank, while the Mīsesīrvīlībāz seat is drawn instead from the realm's most senior military officer completing his last tour of deployable command.

A Maegystīrys earned at five-and-twenty proves its holder's judgment once; what keeps the vote thereafter is that judgment's continued exercise. As the Tireless Hand takes up more of the realm's routine labour, more of the work left to a Vysoan in every industry is the work of oversight — calibrating, verifying, and deciding — and so every working Maegystīrys is already an overseer whose judgment is reviewed in the ordinary course of his vocation, under the provisions of The Hand Remembered: the guiding questions at the point of decision, the drills, and the record of his work. His continued performance in the capacity he was certified for, whatever the industry, is the standing proof of his fitness for the ballot. No periodic re-examination is held; recertification is called for only where a critical failure presents itself.

Retirement does not suspend the franchise, for a Vysoan retirement is no idleness. The course of a life turns at that threshold, customarily at seventy, from work and labour to generativity, the retired passing on what they know to those who follow, and many take up the crafts no machine performs as the leisure of their remaining years. Their judgment goes on being exercised, and the vote goes on being kept.

At the moment of casting, the ballot itself puts a few guiding questions to the voter, asking him to confirm the reasons for his choice before it is made. They are not graded and turn no one away; they ask the overseer to check his own result, as every overseer in the realm is asked to do.

A critical failure is a demonstrated inability to perform in one's certified capacity — not a single error, but a failure repeated and costly, as when a production-line manager repeatedly ill-calibrates the line's thinking machine, losing the line time and return. Such a failure is reviewed by a panel of the subject's colleagues and superiors, with an independent arbitrator seated where one is needed. Where the panel finds it, the franchise is suspended while the matter is remedied: the root of the failure is identified, the possible courses of retraining are weighed, and the subject is retrained and recertified. Once recertification is resolved, the subject is restored in full. A failure of this kind costs a Vysoan time, never citizenship.

No body of voters in Vysos votes on a matter it does not understand; the very idea is held unthinkable. Before any Gerialbar decides a question touching a field of work, it consults the actual practitioners of that field, credentialed or not, gathered into expert consultative committees, and draws from them the knowledge required to close its own gap in understanding. The vote follows that understanding and never precedes it. It is through these committees, and through the feedback any practitioner may send up the ranks from any rung, that those who do not vote still shape every decision that touches their work: their knowledge is not merely heard but required before the ballot is cast.

The members of a consultative committee declare their interest in any matter put before them. Fear for one's livelihood is not the concern, for no Vysoan, with retraining ordinary and the Common Floor beneath him, stands to lose his living by a vote. The declaration guards instead against attachment to a practitioner's own methods. Committees are convened as needed, and their members need not be present in the flesh: far-speech serves as well as a seat at the table. No committee speaks for more than its own field, and votes weigh one field against another; that weighing is the work of the Maegystīrys, the synthesiser of the expertise of many fields, and it is the reason the vote is his while the knowledge belongs to all.

The gate to the franchise is held open by the same test that guards it. Admission to a Maegysombāzmion turns on the disposition to rule, as the Covenant defines it, weighed alongside aptitude, never on circumstance; and the record already sets down how that disposition is tested across the whole of the Otāgūrēñion years. A Maegystīrys between posts keeps the franchise, his faculties intact and his hands engaged in a craft. Where a decision cannot wait for a committee to be convened, it rests with the Kardārys.

The Covenant defines that disposition; Vysoan science measures it. The simulated crises of the Otāgūrēñion record a candidate's accuracy, consistency and speed of judgment as the stakes rise, together with the physiological marks of composure, and tasks drawing on evidence from several unfamiliar fields measure his capacity to synthesise. Some five centuries of records, kept since the pathways were codified under Kēlāeriōñ , tie those measures at sixteen to the same subjects' conduct decades later, in office, in the civil service and before the panels of review, so that the realm can show its entrance standard predicts the judgment it is meant to predict, and every review renders further evidence by which the test is refined. The Covenant raises no objection, holding that the Starshaper means knowledge and the sciences to be put to use; it explains why dispositions differ, since they return with the soul, while science shows how they differ. What science cannot settle is what ruling well consists of: that remains the Covenant's to define, and the evidence's to keep honest.

The realm has settled in doctrine, ahead of the day it is needed, that the franchise shall not be opened to beings of other physiology, should Vysos ever meet them among the stars, nor to Autonomous Persons, should its thinking machines ever become persons in their own right, on grounds of the realm's security. The Vysoan system was designed and calibrated for Vysoans; were a species, or an Autonomous Person able to replicate itself, to come to make up a sizeable share of the realm, or to outnumber Vysoans outright, its admission to the vote would leave the realm open to interests not its own. By Vysoan physiology the doctrine means not the Vysoan people alone but any humanoid people of similar lifespan and developmental course the stars may yet reveal, lifespan weighing most; what the rule is meant to prevent is the naturalisation of beings whose timescales and contexts differ so vastly from the realm's own as to be incompatible with it by default. A naturalised migrant of Vysoan physiology who has completed the recalibration of mindset and attitude naturalisation will ask of him may hold the franchise. The Maegysombāzmioni are to recognise foreign institutions and certifications; what such a migrant must pass are the key checks a Maegysombāzmion education exists to develop: the ability to synthesise, and judgment under pressure. A child of mixed parentage, one parent of Vysoan physiology, is to be eligible in the same way; one not educated on Vȳsōs must first undergo the same recalibration. Those barred from the vote are not to be barred from counsel: beings of other physiology, and Autonomous Persons, may serve on the consultative committees of the trades they practise, their knowledge heard though they cast no ballot.

Election is not the last check a Jovertys answers to: the Magistracy of Vettsīrdārdrīvo maintains a standing court at each of the five levels, empowered to examine a Jovertys's own decision on its merits regardless of what the electing Gerialbar makes of it. The Dēmōndosēr answers to no such court — his own decisions stand checked by nothing beneath the Kardārys himself.

The Palace

The Mount and the WatersThe Grand StairwayThe Outer CourtThe Dragonpits and the LairsThe Main CourtThe Hall of StateThe Inner CourtRaising the MountThe MagistraciesThe Order of Heights
Plan of the summit, front at the foot

The reclaimed island beneath it all runs to some 750 square kilometres, room enough beyond the halls of state for parks, markets, museums, and the ordinary residential quarters of those who serve the crown daily rather than merely visit it. Its coastline is irregular rather than geometric, reading in outline as a rough, canted diamond — four uneven points toward the compass's own cardinals, no one corner square and no two alike. The mount stands at the island's own centre, ringed by that reclaimed ground on every side. The palace stands upon a mount raised by hand, forty-nine stories above the ground, and is reached on foot by a single stair of 777 steps. Its summit divides into three courts laid one behind another along a single axis: the outer court of arrival, the main court of state, and the inner court of the royal household. Each threshold admits fewer than the last, so that the plan itself enacts the order of the court.

Three ways of arriving are kept apart. Those on foot climb the stair; ministers, dignitaries and others permitted air travel alight on the forecourt; riders descend by dragon into the dragonpits and proceed along avenues of their own.

The Mount and the Waters#

The mount measures 1,600 by 1,300 metres at the ground and rises 147 metres. It is laid square to the compass: its front faces north toward Zobrezos, from whose shore it was raised, and its rear faces south. Those two faces slope inward some 71 degrees, each setting back 50 metres, while its long flanks, east and west, stand sheer; the summit thus measures 1,500 by 1,300 metres. A wall 10 metres high rings the summit, secluding the court, breaking the wind, and crowning the cliff when seen from below. Only the buildings rising above it command the panorama.

A moat 65 metres wide encircles the mount, enclosing 1,730 by 1,430 metres and holding some 39.4 hectares of water. A bridge 130 metres wide crosses it to the foot of the stair. Four waterfalls, two upon each flank, pour from the jaws of sun-gold dragons' heads, framing the Barsīvōñ on one side and the Great Hall of the People on the other, and fall 147 metres into the moat. A fifth and greatest cascade falls at the centre of the rear face. Pumps draw the moat's water back to the summit, so that the palace's waters run as a single circuit.

The Grand Stairway#

The stair is cut 130 metres wide into the front of the mount and climbs between the two forward wings of the outer court. Its steps carry a 30-centimetre tread and a rise of about 18.9 centimetres, a pitch of some 32 degrees. Six landings, each 16.15 metres deep, divide it into seven flights of 111 steps, each flight rising seven stories (21 metres) over a run of 33.3 metres. From foot to head the stair runs 330 metres, emerging 280 metres behind the summit's front edge.

The walls of the cutting stand deepest, about 125 metres, where the stair pierces the front face, and fall away to nothing at its head. A pair of sun-gold dragons, each 18 metres tall, stands on either side of every landing, gazing down on those who climb: twelve in all. The ascent takes a visitor of ordinary health some 25 to 35 minutes and ends at the first gate of the palace proper.

The Outer Court#

The outer court is 400 metres deep. Beyond the head of the stair a forecourt 120 metres deep opens directly onto the two forward wings, each 585 metres wide, and leads to the central gate into the main court. The central 130 metres of the forecourt are kept clear as the stair's processional continuation.

On either side of that way lie twelve landing pads, 25 metres square, in four columns and three rows across an area 151.25 by 120 metres: twenty-four pads in all, flush with the paving and without towers or hangars. Each group has its own guard post and checkpoint. Aircraft approach along the line of the stair's gorge, clear of the dragons descending over the pits.

Those four-and-twenty pads are the ordinary way up the mount for anyone not riding a dragon of his own — cleared by the Lord High Equerry’s own office for whichever shuttle or skiff a courtier arrives in, and withdrawn by that same office on a word from the Kardārys alone, no reason given or asked. A courtier who finds his own clearance quietly revoked has no second way up but the stair itself: the full 330 metres of it, and the five-and-twenty to five-and-thirty minutes the climb is reckoned to take, arriving before whatever business awaited him in whatever state that climb has left him in. No censure is ever entered against a name for it, and the Kardārys is rarely troubled to explain himself; the stair, and the state a man arrives in, explain it for him.

The rest of the wings belong to the dragonkeepers, laid out identically on both sides. Along the summit's outer edge and the rim of the gorge, a way 32.5 metres wide runs between two bands of buildings, each 50 metres deep, with a garden strip of 18.75 metres beside each dragonpit's moat. Along the summit's front edge and the wall of the main court, a walk of 16.25 metres runs between rows of smaller buildings 21.25 metres deep. Here stand the keepers' lodges, saddleries and tack houses, riders' halls, a dragon infirmary, armouries, and the offices of the stables under the Lord High Equerry of the Sublime Stables.

The Dragonpits and the Lairs#

Two dragonpits stand at the centres of the outer court's wings, 292.5 metres in from each side of the summit and 200 metres behind its front edge. Each is 250 metres across, its floor sunk 112 metres below the summit, 35 metres above the ground outside. Above the summit, each rises in three concentric rings of arches in the manner of an ancient amphitheatre, the outer ring highest and each ring within one arcaded tier lower than the last:

RingRadiusHeight above summitForm
Outer112.5–125 m73.5 mThree arcaded tiers of 18 m and an attic of 19.5 m
Second100–112.5 m54 mThree arcaded tiers
Inner87.5–100 m36 mTwo arcaded tiers
Oculuswithin 87.5 mOpen175 m across, closable by a swift retracting cover

Every ring carries 80 arches, one each 4.5 degrees, aligned radially from the outer wall inward; the terraces atop the rings, each 12.5 metres deep, serve as galleries and roosts. All dragons enter and leave by the oculus, which leaves some 20 metres' clearance on either side of a wingspan of 135 metres, the measure of the greatest dragons. Riders and handlers come and go by a pair of lifts, each about 4 by 4 metres, and provisions by a freight lift of about 10 by 10 metres. A moat 16.25 metres wide encircles each pit.

The lairs lie beneath the main court's two flanks, each 435 by 700 metres, at the pits' floor level, in vaulted halls 60 metres tall; a band 430 metres wide beneath the centre is kept for the hall of state's foundations, the monarch's private tunnel, and the waterworks. Passages 50 by 50 metres lead from each pit's floor to its lairs. A secondary exit runs some 450 metres beneath the inner court to an opening about 100 metres wide in the mount's rear face, hidden behind the great rear waterfall; at need a mechanism halts the water and opens the way for rider and dragon.

The Main Court#

The main court, 700 metres deep, lies at the exact centre of the summit and holds the palace's buildings of state. Three parallel avenues, each 65 metres wide, run through it: the central axis from the forecourt to the inner court, and a dragon avenue on either side, centred 292.5 metres in from the summit's edge, which issues from the rear gate of each dragonpit, passes through the wall into the main court, and continues into the inner court. Lateral avenues cross the court at its midpoint from the causeways of the hall of state to the Barsīvōñ and the Great Hall of the People.

Canals 16.25 metres wide run beside the avenues rather than within them: from the hall's water ring along both sides of each lateral avenue, along the full inner and outer lengths of each dragon avenue, around each dragonpit's moat, and past the Barsīvōñ and the Great Hall of the People to the four waterfalls of the flanks. Wherever an avenue crosses water, it does so by a raised bridge of seven steps.

The central precinct between the dragon avenues is quartered by the axis and the lateral avenues. In each quarter stand three obelisks in an L, marking three of its corners and leaving the fourth open toward the hall: 49 metres tall, 4.90 metres square at the base, each set 48.75 metres in from its quarter's edges, 178.75 metres apart along the walls and 203.75 metres along the canals. Each is capped by a sun-gold pyramidion and serves as a flue from the lairs below; on ceremonial occasions smoke issues from beneath the gilded tip, and at other times it is turned aside through the dragonpits' oculi.

The Hall of State and Its Island

The hall of state stands within a circular garden 150 metres in radius, ringed by a pathway 65 metres wide: a lane of water 32.5 metres across, brimming 0.15 metres below promenades of 16.25 metres on either side, the whole circle measuring 430 metres. Trees line both edges at every 3 degrees, open within 12 degrees of each causeway. Four causeways, each 65 metres wide, cross the water at the cardinal points, each rising by seven steps of 15 centimetres to a deck 1.05 metres above the promenades, its underside clearing the water by 0.2 metres.

Along the water's centre, at every 15 degrees save the four cardinal points, rise twenty fountains in basins 12 metres across: a column of 6 metres guarded on four sides by sun-gold dragons 3 metres tall, water pouring from their jaws, crowned by a sun in splendour 3 metres across cast in sun-gold, veiled in the mist falling from its rays.

The Barsīvōñ and the Great Hall of the People

Facing one another across the court at the ends of the lateral axis stand two identical domed halls, each 240 by 130 metres and rising to 82.5 metres, three quarters the height of the hall of state. On the left, upon the eastern side and facing west, stands the Barsīvōñ — the Hall of Seven Lights — raised by Āeñāriōñ and dedicated to the memory of Rāehaerys , the great temple and headquarters of the Sidereal Covenant; on the right, upon the western side and facing east, the Great Hall of the People — the Karjiōrionēr Ābrēr — where both houses of the Gerialbar, the Āeksiōrion and the Qupteōrion, convene. Faith and legislature thus flank the throne, with the hall of state standing between them.

Every other temple in Vysos follows the Barsīvōñ's pattern. Its drum and dome are repeated in each to the same proportions and the same layout, only at smaller scale: the square drum and the dome above it, the temple floor upon its pillars, the seven chapels of the star in the order of the Seven, the galleries of the Ēlvesēli and the Orderers' rotunda, and the levels of niches below. Every temple is also oriented as the Barsīvōñ is: its front faces west, with the high altar and great window at the east, so that the faithful look eastward toward the altar and the window takes the morning sun. The rule holds for every temple in Vysos, whatever its site. A worshipper who knows his parish temple can find his way about the Barsīvōñ, and the reverse holds as well. The wings are not repeated. They house the offices and archives of the Covenant's headquarters and belong to the Barsīvōñ alone.

Each temple's niches receive the dead of its own province, and the nobility are ordinarily laid to rest there or in their family mausoleums. Interment in the Barsīvōñ is an honour rather than a right of birth: it is granted for distinction to nobles, clergy and commoners alike. By custom, about a hundred places are granted each year, fewer than one death in half a million across the realm. At that rate the Barsīvōñ's 234,000 niches, opened in the reign of its builder, hold only some four thousand of the honoured dead by RŌĀ 1017, and are reckoned to receive the realm's distinguished for more than two thousand years to come. The imperial family rests in its own mausoleum.

The stately residences each enclose a courtyard of 40 by 40 metres. Every residence is bordered on all four sides by a way 10 metres wide.

The Hall of State#

At the exact centre of the main court, and so of the whole palace, stands the hall of state: a square base 119.70 metres a side and 28.17 metres tall, rising to a dome 95 metres across whose crown reaches 110.25 metres above the courts and 257.25 metres above the ground. A glazed oculus 17.48 metres across opens at the crown of an interior worked in elaborate art.

The hall is built in stories of 4.5 metres. The first level holds the grand reception hall for lords and visiting dignitaries; the second, the great hall of state dinners and banquets; each rises 13.5 metres. Enclosed stairwells stand at the four corners, the front pair rising to the throne level and the rear pair stopping at the second; corridors 5 metres wide encircle both lower levels.

The throne level, from 27 metres, is reached only by the front stairwells, which open onto a corridor along the front and a central doorway into the rotunda. Around the rotunda's circumference stand 38 sun-gold statues, one for each king who has reigned, 19 on either side in groups of 10 and 9, each 6 to 8 metres tall and about 3.1 metres apart. A straight walkway crosses the rotunda to the throne, set in a niche 10.64 metres wide and 19 metres tall at the centre of the rear wall, within a throne room 10 metres deep. Doorways at the rotunda's left and right open onto two council rooms of 20 by 10 metres, each with 37.5 metres of antechambers and offices on either side. Private passages 2.35 metres wide run in an L along the side and rear walls, joining the council rooms, the rear-corner antechambers and their private stair, and a concealed door behind the throne.

Nineteen flying buttresses ring the hall, each rising from a pier 6 metres square set 6 metres from the wall, 14.95 metres apart: five upon each side and the rear, and four upon the front, where the inner pair frame the main door 35.90 metres apart. Their arches brace the dome at its springing, and each pier is crowned by a pinnacle. The central pier of the rear conceals the monarch's lift, rising from a private tunnel toward the inner court to an enclosed passage bridging to the rear wall; that passage serves as a hidden antechamber, from which the Kardārys may step directly into the throne niche.

The Inner Court#

The inner court, 400 metres deep, holds the royal household. At its head, upon the axis, stands the imperial residence, spanning 480 metres: a central square of 130 metres and two curved wings, each a sector of about 60 degrees, 70 metres deep, reaching forward to embrace the court. The residence rises six floors of 4.9 metres to a main body of 29.4 metres, holding some 2,000 rooms. Over the square rises a ribbed dome upon a lofty drum with a lantern, 52 metres across, its crown 88.2 metres above the summit, second in height only to the hall of state.

Between the residence and the main court, flanking the axis, stand the two barracks of the Solar Scions, each a quadrant-shaped building of 170 by 130 metres, so that none approaches the monarch's home without passing between them. The dragon avenues curve into the inner court as an arc before the residence, lined on both sides with trees planted at equal angular intervals and kept below the residence's main body.

Two pools flank the residence and feed the great rear waterfall. In the rear corners, on either side, lie the monarch's private gardens, their paths lined with trees in a freer planting of shaded walks and groves. Beneath them, within the mount, lie the concealed quarters of the palace staff. Provisions for the court arrive by air.

Raising the Mount#

The mount's own base — barely two square kilometres against the island's 750 — is driven up from the sea floor first and separately: consolidation and fill occupy some three years, the retaining walls and summit's own footing a further five, so that the raised base stands clear of the water within the reign's first decade. The halls, courts, pits, and towers that follow it — the hall of state's dome capped last and highest of all — take a further dozen years, leaving the mount entire finished within some twenty years of Āeñāriōñ 's accession, comfortably inside his own thirty-year reign. The wider island is slower business: its full 750 square kilometres are not wholly settled — parks, markets, and residential quarters filled in behind the mount's own works — until a decade and more beyond its completion, spreading on into the reign of his son, Āedāriōñ .

The Magistracies#

Beyond the moat, scattered across the rest of the reclaimed island rather than gathered in any one place, stand the fifteen spires of the Maegysdārarziēri, one for each Maegysdārarz the Qrogorjentys seats. Each rises upwards of 1,000 metres and holds at least 200 levels, every level given over to ordinary office space; among the tallest structures standing anywhere in Zobrezos, they answer to no ceremonial precedence and so are free to clear the hall of state several times over.

Two further towers stand among them, raised for the Gaomajenti of the realm's twin Agencies — Domestic and Galactic Intelligence — low and broad rather than tall, neither reaching for the Maegysdārarziēri's own height. Each rises octagonal in plan, echoing the Vysoan crest, as a stack of concentric rings, each smaller and set higher than the one below; every ring's eight faces are further divided into eight panels by a narrow gap left at each of the octagon's own points.

The Supreme Court stands apart from both Chair and Magistracy and above the Magistracy's own standing courts, the realm's court of final appeal: a squarish block with four corner spires — each spire's outer quarter jutting clear of the block itself to form an L where tower meets building.

The Treasury keeps no single vault; its reserves are scattered instead across Vȳsōs and the stations of the Vēzos system, in vaults whose number, description, and location go unpublished.

The island's centre of learning is the Great Library of Ēlyrōz the Erudite, raised by Ēlyrōz at Uēpoktio beside the first Maegysombāzmion and given its present seat here when Āeñāriōñ built the island. The complex measures 500 by 500 metres upon a base rising seven storeys from the ground; its main building, square at 250 by 250 metres, carries a rotunda and dome. At each of the complex's four corners stands an L-shaped secondary library, its galleries 100 metres long, open ground left between each outer library and the main one; all four sides admit entry, each by both stair and travelator.

The Peerage

The Sixteen RanksThe Twenty Vēzghare Eglentroti

By RŌĀ 1017 the peerage is purely ceremonial. Nobles keep their titles, precedence, and incomes, but neither day-to-day administrative governance — which belongs to the Qrogorjentys (see The Crown & Government) — nor command of men-at-arms beyond a personal household guard, soldiers answering to crown officers rather than noble banners. Titles are retained deliberately, as status, heritage, and royal-favor currency; their holders keep the right to be consulted by the crown officials now administering their former demesnes, along with a portion of that income. Their real political leverage runs through the Āeksiōrion, the upper house the peerage elects from among its own number.

Counted by house rather than by rank, the peerage of RŌĀ 1017 stands some four thousand five hundred strong: twenty houses Vēzghare Eglentroti, high houses of the sun-blood; eighty Eglentroti, high houses proper; four hundred Lentroti, houses of the middle nobility; and four thousand Arlentroti, new houses of the low nobility.

The Sixteen Ranks#

The peerage runs five tiers, sixteen ranks in all:

Above even the Sixteen Ranks stands Kardāryñ, Empress — the feminine form of the throne's own title, Kardārys, held by his consort rather than by a woman reigning as sovereign in her own right, presently held by Jaenanne Qelosiñe, consort to Āeñāriōñ . Their formal High Vysoan styles stand recorded also: Ȳse Kardārōñe Rōvegliss, "His Imperial Majesty," for the Kardārys, and Ȳñ Kardārōñe Rōvegliss, "Her Imperial Majesty," for the Kardāryñ — the feminine formula rightly takes the bare pronoun Ȳñ rather than the genitive Ȳñe, since Ȳñe would read as "Hers Imperial Majesty" rather than "Her Imperial Majesty," exactly as Common Vysoan itself distinguishes the two.

Royalty — Kardārilaros/Kardārilēsyñ, Kardārlisos/Kardārlisyñ, Dārlisos/Dārlisyñ Kardārōgare. A Kardārlisos/Kardārlisyñ (Imperial Prince/Princess) is measured within four generations of a reigning Kardārys at the holder's own birth — a measure fixed for life, not recalculated as reigns pass.

High Nobility — Ēlvalys/Ēlvalyñ, Kardrāzantys/Kardrāzantyñ, Drāzantys/Drāzantyñ.

Middle Nobility — Pāleqiros/Pāleqiryñ, Grozqiros/Grozqiryñ, Oktiqiros/Oktiqiryñ, Lenqiros/Lenqiryñ.

Low Nobility — Byqiros/Byqiryñ, Jezantys/Jezantyñ, Valzantys/Valzantyñ.

Honorifics — Vēzīrigomēr, Mīzantys Pāsābarie, Mīzantys Maegysombāzmione — the last held since its creation by House Vēzegsīdōr, for the close relationship the Vēzegsīdōri have maintained with the Maegysombāzmioni since Ēlyrōz founded the first of them (see History).
