Insignia & Heraldry

The Crown's VestmentsWhat Flies Over Vysos

The Crown's Vestments#

The Kardārys's state dress is distinct from, and set above, the Order's own black-and-gold war dress: an under-robe of sun-gold, worked densely in fine scrollwork and carrying the house's own two-headed dragon as a facing pair of serpents; a stiff gold collar and gold shoulder roundels, a wide gold belt set with rubies, and a cape of unrelieved black, worn open and asymmetrically from the right shoulder, bordered throughout in the same gold scrollwork. Bracers of dark Vȳsōmēdon each carry a single raised sunburst medallion; his boots are plain black. A long gold scepter, headed by a ruby-set sunburst, is carried rather than worn, and Brightflame itself rides at his side, hidden beneath the cape. The crown itself is a plain Vȳsōmēdon circlet banded in sun-gold, with four sets of large dragon wings curving upward at the cardinal points to nearly meet overhead, a smaller mirrored set beneath each, every vein embossed in gold — where the fans nearly close, the tracery gathers into a solar motif with a Vȳsōmēdon dragon's head at its heart, facing outward at each of the four directions — the form the throne's crown has settled toward across the generations, though custom has never bound a reign to it: how the fixed material and vocabulary are worked into a crown's own shape has always been each king's own choice, and Āeñāriōñ 's own crown runs plainer — a circlet rising to a shallow point at every quarter, one pair of stylised wings flanking a central finial set with a single ruby, rather than the four great fans and their ruby-set seams — no more binding on the Kardārys after him than the fuller form was on him, and no more without precedent than it is on him.

What Flies Over Vysos#

Three tiers of flag fly across the realm, all built from the shield's own tinctures — sun-gold, a black near enough to Vȳsōmēdon to share its name, and a house red older than the Covenant's own sigil. The System flag, gold with black-and-red pallets at hoist and fly, is the one every merchantman and household actually flies, belonging to Vēzos before it belongs to any throne, and the one flag that still lets a single sun stand in for the whole shield. The Kardārys's own personal standard answers to the Order's own treatment: black, crossed edge to edge by a gold sunburst with a smaller sunburst set in each corner, framed by a red-and-gold bordure, flying only where he is physically present and struck the moment he leaves. The Solar Scions fly a banner built from the sun entire in gold and red rather than gold and black, rays running edge to edge with no ground left bare, closed by a thin black-and-gold bordure. An octagonal roundel, gold or black, marks hulls, wings, and uniforms in place of any flag's finer detail — the black version serving the Order's own markings, a hull mark answering to settled convention rather than to whichever colours a service flies.

Two emblems divide the realm's imagery between them. The sun stands for Vysos itself, the realm and its people, and so it is the sun that runs freely through civil dress, public works and the everyday aesthetic of the realm, which leans far more to the solar than to the draconic. The dragon stands for the throne and the House of Vēzgharyōñ, and is kept to the crown, the house and what belongs to them, much as the prefix Kar- is kept to the house's own names. The Kardārys alone bears both rightly, Son of the Sun and Dragon of the Void at once, for the throne he holds rules the realm it stands for.

Beneath the King's own standard the armed forces fly three war ensigns, one for the united service, one for the army, one for the fleet, each bearing the same fuller badge the Kardārys's own standard and the Scions' banner carry — an octagon, an eight-pointed star, and the house's sun-and-dragon roundel together, always cast in gold regardless of field. The armed forces' own ensign is the boldest of the three: an eight-pointed burst of red and black run clean to the cloth's edge, unbordered, answering to no other flag. The Army's colour is quartered instead, per saltire in red and black within a black-and-gold border — a shield's own geometry for a colour meant to be studied at close range rather than glimpsed once across open water. The Navy's ensign doubles the badge's own sixteen rays to two-and-thirty, narrower and more numerous than any other flag of the realm, so the alternation still resolves at a masthead's distance. None of the three shares the gold-or-black hull-marking roundel above, since none of their own fields reads wholly as one tincture or the other; instead all three services wear a single Service Roundel in common, the fuller achievement worn whole rather than reduced to the plainer sun and wyvern the hull mark carries.

PreviousThe PeerageNextThe Solar Scions
Part V · Sword and Order · Section 10 of 15

The Solar Scions

The Order's Own ReckoningWhat Blood Carries Forward

The Kardārōñe Qogrorāzma Vēzenkelarie — the Imperial Military Order of the Solar Scions — is a chivalric military order nominally held under the Eglābaros's religious jurisdiction but commanded, day to day, by a Jendrāzys (Order Commander) and, in final authority, by the Kardārys himself. Its origin is native and older than its charter: it grew from the gifted seers of the flame, the Ūndissari, who scried the Starshaper's visions in the temple fires of the Sidereal Covenant long before any king gathered them under his own command, and from the gifted of the royal blood, in whom the same gift that once let the Zaldrāeksi bond their dragons still woke in each generation (see Doctrine & Religion). Founding was two-staged — Kēlāeriōñ (RŌĀ 455–484) gathered seers and gifted princes alike into a standing crown institution; his successor in the work, Valkarōz (RŌĀ 679–710), codified its rule, branches, attire, and oath into the form still kept in RŌĀ 1017, and formalised the seers' sole claim on prophecy. In the years between, Rāethor sent the Order's adepts to cleanse the shattered Valiērian peninsula, the first work of the realm the Scions carried out as a body. Since Kēlāeriōñ gathered it, every gifted Vysoan has been inducted into the Order exclusively — a practice Valkarōz 's codification made fixed rule — no temple, house, or guild permitted to train the gift outside it; the Sīvoktyr priesthood no longer numbers the gifted among its own, and prophecy — receiving the Starshaper's visions, and interpreting them — belongs to the Order alone.

The Order's Own Reckoning#

The Order's bar has never been blood, only the gift — Elaenyra Ūndembreys herself stands a trained Scion by right of her own visions rather than by Vēzgharyōñ descent, precedent enough that no serving Scion doubts the principle. Extended to whatever peoples the realm may yet meet among the stars, the same logic answers before the court's own has finished asking: a gifted subject of the throne would be eligible for the oath regardless of what he was born looking like, since the Starshaper's gift is handed out by neither house nor kind — a view the Ūndissari, receiving the Starshaper's visions directly with no bloodline test attached, hold most settled of all. The Jorgūrēnti part from the court's comfortable curiosity here: knowledge-gathering is their whole calling, not a diplomatic nicety, so a Seeker sent among the remote and unlettered peoples of Vȳsōs's own far shores feels the realm's general unease toward strangers more sharply than any courtier, tempered by a caution born of actually walking among such peoples rather than merely receiving their envoys — knowledge taken without being earned is rarely given twice. The Jurnazanti judge a stranger by steadiness under pressure and skill at arms sooner than by lineage or legacy.

Four branches divide its work, each answering to one of the gift's permitted reaches — telekinesis, telepathy, astral projection, and scrying, of which prophecy and flame-seeing are but forms: the Jurnazanti ("Sentinels," combat specialists, whose Vēzgharzantys — "Sunblood Sentinels" — serve as the Kardārys's personal bodyguard), the Ūndissari ("Seers," who commune with the Starshaper and receive prophecy without interpreting it), the Drīvāpagi ("Secernators," who discern the correct interpretation of a Seer's vision), and the Jorgūrēnti ("Seekers," who gather temporal and mystical knowledge across Vȳsōs and the Vēzos system, and are charged to carry that search beyond it as the realm enters the stars). Everyday dress is a black inner tunic beneath a golden tabard, cinched with a sash into which a Scion's blade is thrust; combat branches add form-fitting black weave, bronze-and-Vȳsōmēdon plate in draconic and solar motifs, and a matching helm, while the Seer and Secernator branches wear a plainer black-weave robe and woven harness. Older tales credit the first seers with healing by the gift and with killing shadows; the Order teaches both as legend, unproven, and claims neither.

Every full Scion is issued a sunblade at initiation, standard to the whole Order and built to a single pattern, forged of Vȳsōmēdon ("Vysos's Steel"), an alloy of Adamant ore whose forging method is a closely guarded state secret. Its crossguard spreads two sun-gold dragon wings outward from the blade; a Vȳsōmēdon knob rings the grip beneath for a surer hold; the hilt itself is grooved along its length; and the pommel closes in a flame shaped like an egg, worked whole in sun-gold. The blade a Scion draws marks his calling in the flame inlaid along its fuller: the Jurnazanti and Jorgūrēnti carry orange, the Ūndissari and Drīvāpagi magenta. Brightflame, the Kardārys's own sunblade, stands apart from this standard pattern as the throne's own heirloom rather than an issued weapon: a ribbed Vȳsōmēdon handle, a sun-gold guard shaped as four dragon wings meeting roaring dragon heads at each face, a sun-gold pommel gripping a red-orange stone in four clawed settings, and a blade whose temper shows orange from a distance with a tinge of red at its edge on close inspection — worn at the King's side, hidden beneath his outer cape.

What Blood Carries Forward#

Mind is held formed chiefly by raising rather than by blood or flesh alone — the same principle, differently applied, that lets a foundling raised under a stranger's roof claim a mind fully his own. Blood's role is narrower: it furnishes, through lineage, the household a mind is raised within. Blood keeps one office the raising cannot discharge for it, however: it is what a house's record is a record of. Membership in a house is a matter of descent entered and traceable — the same witnessed record by which the realm trusts only what it can verify — and the gift running in the Vēzgharyōñ line runs by that descent alone. A mind raised under a house's roof may take on that house's cast, as a fostered child is meant to; it can never take on the house's descent, which is why fostering is honoured and adoption is not. House Vēzgharyōñ reads as the plainest case — a prince or princess raised amid a household shaped, generation upon generation, by an accumulation of the Starshaper's gift few families can match comes to carry forward a portion of ancestral temperament and cast of mind by that raising alone, setting the royal mentality apart from the common subject's. It is the same reasoning that already holds the Order better suited than an ordinary family to raise a gifted child. None of this is troubled by the plain possibility of an heir born without the gift: his standing within the succession is unchanged, since formation by household needs only the household's own accumulated cast of mind, not the gift itself — though after so many generations of marriage concentrated within a bloodline this steeped in the Starshaper's own light, the chance of it is held vanishingly small.

The Scion's Oath — sworn in unison

"We profess faith in the Starshaper most high, Maker of the Stars, who through the Seven lights the way, and banishes the night... We are an instrument of the Starshaper. Where there is discord, let us bring peace; where there is chaos, harmony... and where there is darkness, light. We are the flame that warms, the light that brings the dawn. To our God and King, we give our lives. To their will, we pledge our blades. This day and all our days to come. Cast your light upon us, O Starshaper, and bear witness. Ōsar Vēzos Mazīl Daor — Our Sun Sets Not."

The Military

Ships, Fleets, and EchelonsThe Line and the SpecialistThe One-and-Twenty GradesWhat the Services Wear

Ships, Fleets, and Echelons#

The armed forces settled into their present configuration under Āeñāriōñ , in the first months of his reign, as the realm took up the first hyperdrive engineered under his father Āedāriōñ . The Navy is young, as a realm only now crossing between the stars must have it: the home fleet's sublight ships serve within the Vēzos system, a single test vessel has made the realm's first jump, and the first drive-fitted hulls are building on the slips. The Vysoan Navy reckons seven classes of vessel, named for what each does rather than for its size alone, and sorted into the five categories by which it measures any fleet: the Dreadnought, the Battleship, the Cruiser, the Escort, and the Transport.

High VysoanLiteral TranslationCommon Vysoan
KarizūgadaororGreat To Fear NothingDreadnought (great pattern)
IzūgadaororTo Fear NothingDreadnought
LōgorvīlībāzeShip of BattleBattleship
ĪligomērOne That CrossesCruiser
SolsētegȳzMade to SailEscort (frigate pattern)
AderēbasFast TravellerEscort (corvette pattern)
RāerēbasTraveller That HoldsTransport

The Rāerēbas is the class the realm's reach most depends on: an unarmed or lightly armed hull built to hold rather than to strike, carrying soldiers, colonists, stores and ore between Vȳsōs, the colony on Vēzperzyon and the extraction stations of the system, and in time beyond it. It sails under escort, and its officers are drawn from the same ladder as any warship's.

The capital ships the Navy will build in time are designed around a spinal weapon called the coil-driver: a mass driver running most of the length of the hull, its barrel a long succession of electromagnetic coils that fire in sequence as a dense projectile passes, accelerating it to a significant fraction of the speed of light. The ship aims the weapon by aiming itself. Its power is drawn from the reactor through capacitor banks charged between shots, so that it fires heavy, deliberate blows rather than a barrage.

The weapon suits the realm. It asks for electricity, coils and dense metal, all of which Vysoan refineries and foundries supply in abundance, and its slugs can be manufactured by the thousand from the ore of the extraction stations. Its coils must fire in perfect sequence across hundreds of stages, a precision the inspectorate verifies to tolerance. At such speed a few kilograms carry the force of a heavy warhead, concentrated on a single point. It is a weapon for breaking stations and capital ships, and the realm's doctrine binds it to targets in space alone: under the organic command that governs every opening of hostilities, a coil-driver is never turned upon a world.

Beyond the coil-driver the realm sets a greater work among its far ambitions. It means one day to build a Dyson swarm, a vast array of collectors in independent orbit about Vēzos, the system's own star, gathering its output, and it plans it first and plainly as a means of providing energy and power: a public utility on the scale of the realm's ambitions, drawing on the star's output without spending the star. As planned, the swarm would leave clear the band of Vȳsōs's orbit and those of the system's other worlds, so that the worlds of Vēzos keep their daylight. It remains a design and a doctrine, not a work begun.

Above the single hull, the Navy groups its ships into five graded formations, each defined by the work it is formed to do rather than by a count of vessels.

High VysoanLiteral TranslationCommon Vysoan
GiezbēvumptisWhole Arrangement To HoverSystem Fleet — the whole of the Navy's strength in a system, under one command
BēvumptisTo HoverFleet — a force of every category, able to act alone and keep itself supplied

BykabēvumptisLittle To HoverFlotilla — a handful of escorts or transports set to a single task

The Army itself is built in ten graded formations, each defined by the role it plays in the one above it; the old numbers in some of their names are kept as names, not as counts.

The Military answers to the Magistracy of Mīsesīrvīlībāz and, through it, to the Kardārys in his Jentys Pāsābarie style; the Solar Scions sit outside this chain of command entirely, sworn to the throne directly.

The Line and the Specialist#

In the army and the security forces alike (the police, and the forces of general public safety), automatons are deployed for the standardised and routine work of arms that the realm's rudimentary thinking machines can bear: sentry, patrol, surveillance and the like. Organic soldiers hold the line of battle and the specialised forces, each supported by accompanying automatons where the machines can serve, for the work in which an organic soldier's judgement and presence still bear upon the outcome; doctrine already looks ahead to the day automatons may stand in the line itself, and sets down now how that day is to be governed.

The dragons have no place in this order. A dragon is no match for the guns of a modern army, still less for a ship, and the realm's own wars long ago proved them obsolete on the field; were one ever pressed into service, it would serve at most as a mount for gifted specialised infantry. In practice they are ceremonial: the royal dragons fly at coronations, jubilees and the great feasts of the Covenant, and the crown keeps them as it keeps the regalia, as a bond with the realm's own past rather than a weapon.

The gravest decision is kept in organic hands. The opening of hostilities, and the rules under which automatons may use lethal force, are set by organic command; automatons act within those rules, and anything that falls outside them is referred to an organic officer rather than decided by the machines.

The One-and-Twenty Grades#

Rank runs a twenty-one-code ladder (OF-10 down to OR-1), Navy sections ordered before their Army counterparts at every tier. No grade sits above OF-10: a single Captain General (Army) or Captain Admiral (Navy) commands the realm's top formation outright. Five rungs share identical terms across both services — Ēlvesjenongūrys (OR-10), Uēpajenongūrys (OR-9), and Jenongūrys (OR-8) at warrant tier, Ēlves Jorrālion (OF-1-1) and Tȳnves Jorrālion (OF-1-2) at junior-officer tier — glossed once to cover both branches' distinct functions. The codes are the realm's own grade codes, OF for officers and OR for other ranks; the tenth enlisted rung, OR-10, was added deliberately for the senior warrant grade the two services share. "Jorrālion" itself is a productive deputy or vice-rank modifier, translated "Placeholder."

What the Services Wear#

Five dress categories, common to both services, escalate from the newest recruit to each service's own OF-10, marking rank in the same red-rising-to-gold logic the peerage and civilian dress already use. Full Dress — service dress's own tunic and cap thrown about with a crimson-lined cape from the right shoulder — is reserved for courts, investitures, and state functions, its aiguillette and ribbon rack thickening by seniority until the laurelled cap and fullest rack single out the Captain Admiral or Captain General alone. Service dress — a peaked cap and tunic, red cap-band and collar rank marks climbing to gold — is worn by officers at parade, in the mess, and aboard ship in port. Duty dress trades the peaked cap for an antenna-crowned helmet, issued for garrison rounds and other out-of-base peacetime service, chiefly by enlisted subjects. Battle Armor — segmented plate, ammunition harness, sidearm — is worn on combat, guard, and sentry duty, gold reserved for the two most senior figures alone. Void and Close-Quarters Armor is the same plate fully sealed, an elongated rebreather mask standing in for the open helmet, issued for boarding actions and engagements where the air cannot be trusted, in vacuum or a compromised hull alike; Vysos fields no separate void uniform, only the one it already has, sealed. Every rank in every category wears the Service Roundel fixed to the right sleeve, the one mark common to Army, Navy, and the Armed Forces entire; only the service's own Captain Admiral or Captain General — the sole OF-10 — wears the laurel trace that marks the topmost figure in each dress.

How a Vysoan Is Taught

Foundational SchoolingPathway SchoolingTertiary StudyBeyond the ClassroomThe Reason Behind the RuleThe Founding Game

Schooling runs twenty years in all, reckoned against a natural lifespan of some eighty-five years and a working life that customarily closes at seventy, and carried across three tiers that build on one another rather than standing apart: a shared foundation every subject walks the same ten years of, a five-year fork that first asks which kind of work will claim him, and a five-year tertiary door that answers it. The scheme grew in two steps. Ēlyrōz , the Erudite (RŌĀ 393–405), founded the first Maegysombāzmion at Uēpoktio and tied the suffrage to its graduates of five-and-twenty and over; Kēlāeriōñ , the Great (RŌĀ 455–484), founded the first Sētegombāzmioni and Botȳsombāzmioni beside it and codified the three doors, and the schooling that leads to them, into the tri-pathway system the realm still keeps. Assessment throughout runs on coursework and sustained project work rather than examination, which plays only a minor part at any tier — knowing where and how to find what a problem requires matters more than what a graduate can recite, and knowing how to verify that what he has found is actually sound matters just as much, the reason philosophy, rhetoric, and kindred subjects of critical reasoning weigh so heavily throughout. Verification is never solitary here either: a consequential assessment is graded by a review panel rather than one instructor alone, a given grade's teaching staff lending each other the manpower panel review requires.

Foundational Schooling#

Foundational schooling, age 5 to 15, runs entirely through the Ītsgūrēñion, "Little Learning Hall," its ten years split evenly across two five-year bands.

HallAgesSubjects
Ītsgūrēñion, Grades 1–55–10Common Vysoan, High Vysoan, mathematics, the sciences, aesthetics, Personal Formation
Ītsgūrēñion, Grades 6–1011–15+ literature, history, geography, broader aesthetics, essential technologies

Pathway Schooling#

Pathway schooling, age 16 to 20, forks between the Botȳsgūrēñion, "Trade Learning Hall," and the Otāgūrēñion, "Thinking Learning Hall" — not yet a Maegysombāzmion's own instruction, but the grounding its education presumes of most bound for it, its habits of reasoning serving just as well the rarer Otāgūrēñion leaver whose own aptitude instead points toward a Sētegombāzmion.

HallAgesSubjects
Botȳsgūrēñion (trade)16–20Trade apprenticeship, social sciences, craft and performance aesthetics, applied technologies
Otāgūrēñion (academic)16–20Philosophy, rhetoric, social sciences, aesthetics theory

Tertiary Study#

Tertiary study, age 20 to 25, resolves that fork into three equally respected parallel tracks, each answering a different reach of the same questions rather than sitting in a hierarchy above or below the others. No candidate arrives at any of the three with prior training in what it teaches — specialisation proper begins only once a door is chosen, everything before it being general grounding. The three overlap more than their names suggest: the same trade is very often taught behind all three at once, and what actually separates one from another is the aspect of it each is built to weigh, not the subject itself — a Botȳsombāzmion teaches how a thing is done and the technique that does it best; a Sētegombāzmion teaches why it should be done, how best to do it, and who should be chosen to do it; a Maegysombāzmion leaves the how of the work to the other two and teaches what, why, who, where, and when — the widest reckoning of the three, built for conceptualisation, decision, and management.

InstitutionDomainsReach
MaegysombāzmionTrades and professions generally — from law to engineering, from medicine to the piloting of a starship — taught in some measure behind all three doors alike; the subject never differs from one door to the next, only the aspect, set down under Reach.What, Why, Who, Where, When — conceptualisation, decision, management
Sētegombāzmion, the GuildhallWhat, Why, Who, How — trade mastery, leading a team
Botȳsombāzmion, the Trade AcademyWhat alone, How — not a manager of the work but the surest hand at it

The third of the five years, common to all three doors alike, is given to supervised attachment to two companies or organisations bearing on the door's own course of study, six Hūrarli to each in turn, an allowance drawn from each host rather than a fully qualified worker's own wage, its proportion fixed by statute rather than left to a host's own discretion — genuine exposure to working life, and a reference point carried back into the two years of study still remaining. The fifth and final year closes the door in earnest: a single year-long attachment at one company or organisation, carried on that same allowance, in place of the third year's own pair, and graduation itself turns on it quite as much as on coursework — a candidate needs both sound standing across his coursework and a satisfactory appraisal from a supervisory panel seated jointly from his teaching staff and his workplace managers, neither measure sufficient by itself. Each institution takes a hand in placing its own final-year candidates, weighing skills, interests, and demonstrated competencies alike before setting a man with a host for the year, since the placement is meant, where it answers well, to carry him directly into employment there once his course is finished — the fifth year reaching past mere assessment toward a livelihood already secured. The panel that judges a final attachment carries a third seat besides the teaching staff and workplace managers, held by an officer with no stake in the placement — a magistracy inspector, or one drawn from another trade or institution — empowered to set aside a procedurally unsound finding and to hear a candidate's appeal, such appeals resting with the Magistracy of Vettsīrdārdrīvo; nor does the appraisal and a house's wish to retain a candidate settle together, the appraisal being rendered first and the house's own decision to keep him made only once it stands settled.

Beyond the Classroom#

Admission to a Maegysombāzmion turns as much on disposition as on aptitude: the capacity to think and decide unemotionally under pressure is reckoned among the core competencies weighed, tested across the full five years of Otāgūrēñion coursework through simulated crisis and moot-case scenarios rather than any single admission-day ordeal, and scored on the reasoning produced rather than on how composed a candidate happens to appear — a nervous or expressive manner is no bar where the judgment itself holds. It is the same steadiness of mind the realm's own doctrine counsels of every subject facing a weighty choice. The Otāgūrēñion is the ordinary road to a Maegysombāzmion's gates, not the only one: a Botȳsgūrēñion leaver found to possess the requisite aptitude and disposition may enter one in an Otāgūrēñion graduate's stead. Mid-life career retraining is normal across a working life of some forty-five years; all three tertiary institutions also offer short post-graduate courses for the already-credentialed, so a Maegysombāzmion graduate wanting a Botȳsombāzmion's own depth of technique can take a short course alongside his working life rather than a second five-year apprenticeship — the realm builds it this way rather than as one fused door because Vysoans hold mastery to be completed in stages, one subject learned through before the next is begun, and because a working life that outlasts a single trade leaves no need to rush two aspects into one crowded door when working alongside a second aspect, guided by the same find-and-verify discipline schooling already instills, supplies a great deal of it on its own. Solar Scion training sits entirely outside this scheme, beginning as young as five or six and running a decade or more to full standing. None of this is the whole of what a Vysoan mind can do: the system's charge is producing a well-formed, job-ready citizen, not manufacturing poets or philosophers to order, and while creativity and intellectual pursuit are encouraged and given room throughout, schooling supplies only their foundation — the pursuit itself belongs to a subject's own time. Rare is a good idea born under pressure; more often it is the fruit of casual musing and a sudden, unscheduled moment of enlightenment.

The Reason Behind the Rule#

Running through all three tiers is a single formation, meant to produce a mind that holds firm lines and yet answers to their results — one trusting neither clever arithmetic nor a rule kept for its own sake. Six habits carry it.

The first belongs to the foundational years: no doctrine is taught without what it guards against. Personal Formation sets each line of the catechism and the Ledger beside the harm it exists to prevent, so that a child learns not only that a thing is forbidden but what befalls a realm that permits it, and holds the realm's firm lines as load-bearing rather than arbitrary.

The second belongs to the pathway years: both ways a mind can fail are studied, side by side, as history rather than hardship. One body of cases shows harm justified by clever arithmetic; the other shows rules kept faithfully into ruin, the laws Ēlyāegon 's Great Council (RŌĀ 380–390) struck down among them. A student who has examined both trusts neither pure calculation nor the rule held sacred.

The third runs through the Otāgūrēñion's simulated crises: each asks first for a quick judgment, then for a deliberate analysis, and both are scored. Across five years a student watches his own record — how often his first signal proved right, how often deliberation was right to overturn it — and learns when his intuition can be trusted.

The fourth is set in all three tertiary institutions alike: a process that looks ill-conceived is put before the student, and no change to it may be proposed until its reasons have been recovered and sorted as still valid, obsolete, or unknown. It is the same rule the realm applies before any work is handed to the Tireless Hand.

The fifth outlasts schooling: after every decision of consequence, in attachment and in working life, what was expected is set beside what happened and the difference recorded, without blame, so that results continue to answer back long after the last examination. The sixth belongs to the Maegysombāzmion alone: its students set the answers of many peoples to the same problem side by side — Valiērīa and the city states that followed it, Āerakīs, Braedhōs, Sȳndorīa, and the realm's own reigns — asking of each what it got right and where its conclusions outran its premises, for the synthesiser must first learn to draw from all without belonging to any.

The first, fourth and fifth are the formation of every Vysoan, whatever door he passes through; the second, third and sixth belong chiefly to the formation of those who will decide.

The Founding Game#

A standing component of every Maegysombāzmion course is a game: a grand-strategy simulation in which a student founds a young civilisation and governs it — its economy and treasury, its faith and its factions, its lands, its wars and its treaties — across the centuries of its rise. He plays it, analyses what came of his play, and writes papers on the result, each judged, as every consequential piece of Vysoan work is judged, by a review panel rather than one instructor alone. The simulation keeps its own arithmetic out of sight: a student learns its workings as a magistrate learns a realm's, by what his decisions bring about rather than from a manual, which is the very faculty the Maegysombāzmion exists to train.

The game is played in three modes, taken in order. The first is a campaign played alone, in which the student governs Vysos itself as it stood at one of the great turns of its history — the founding of Zobrezos upon the Pryjatājoni, the civil war of Āeñāriōñ and his sister, the wars against Sȳndorīa, the first foothold on the Moon. It is history taught as a counterfactual: his papers measure his choices against those the realm actually made, and the lesson lives in the gap between them — a student who outperforms the record must explain how, and one who falls short learns respect for decisions that once looked obvious, the realm's history handed down to him as dilemmas lived rather than dates recited. The second is a sandbox played alone, on a civilisation of the student's own design: a laboratory, where, with Vysos set aside, a single question can be tested in isolation — whether a heavily taxed collective state can hold its stability, whether a people can rise on the strength of its culture alone — and the paper that follows states its question, runs the experiment, and reports what it found. The third is a sandbox played among peers, each governing a civilisation of his own design: a forum, supplying the one thing no game played alone can, another mind across the table — negotiation, treaties kept and broken, alliances of convenience, and a student's own policies seen through a rival's eyes — its papers asking why an agreement held or why it failed. Since the first hyperdrive, the game's later centuries carry its civilisations out among the stars, and the realm counts the practice as preparation for the peoples it has yet to meet there.

The order is deliberate. The three modes run from inherited history, through controlled experiment, to the full complexity of other actors, which is the arc of an education in statecraft itself; and the campaign comes first because it alone has a fixed answer to measure against, the realm's own record, before a student is trusted with questions that have none. It is also the sixth habit of the formation set down above given a field to practise on: a Maegysombāzmion student who has founded a dozen civilisations, his own among them, has set the answers of many peoples side by side long before he is asked to decide for one.

The realm's wealth at the dawn of the tireless hand: the principle by which its automatons labour and are checked, the infrastructure beneath them, the common floor their returns secure, the Crown's coin and revenue, the certainty Vysos means to offer the stars, and the discipline that keeps organic skill alive beneath it all.

The Tireless Hand and the Independent Eye#

Vysos sets automaton labour to work wherever it can: in any field where it makes no difference to the outcome of a work, or to how that work is received, whether an organic hand performed it. Where the performer's being organic does bear on the outcome or its reception, the work stays with organic hands. Since the first rudimentary thinking machines were built under Vēzāerys (RŌĀ 829–858), the works so given over have been simple processes — sorting, routing, metering, the repetitive stages of manufacture and the keeping of ledgers — and the realm's doctrine of the tireless hand was written to govern that labour as it widens, rather than after it has outgrown the realm's capacity to check it.

Automaton labour in Vysos answers to the same principle of independent checks that runs through every office of the realm. Every work done by automatons is inspected by an independent inspectorate, its automatons built and trained apart from those whose work they examine, so that no machine checks its own reasoning. An organic official ratifies at each turning point — the purpose at the outset, the design before any material is committed, and acceptance at the end — and anything that would change the brief itself is referred back to that official rather than settled by the machines.

Vysos trusts the tireless hand only as far as it trusts the eye that checks it, and it is on that trust that the realm builds its ambitions. The doctrine looks toward a day when a great Vysoan work may be raised from conception to completion by automatons alone, with organic hands reserved for the offices of purpose and ratification; at RŌĀ 1017 that day is a goal the realm prepares for, not a thing its machines can yet do.

The realm's most valuable holdings, as the tireless hand spreads, are its data centres, for they hold the knowledge and the minds by which its automatons work. As with the Treasury's vaults, there are many of them, and their locations are undisclosed, so that no single strike, theft or seizure can take the realm's memory from it.

Nor is the knowledge of how each work is done by hand allowed to pass out of the realm. It is taught as part of formation, so that the organic officials who check and ratify the work of automatons know that work well enough to verify it, and can judge it rightly.

The Sinews of the Tireless Hand#

An economy of tireless hands rests on infrastructure laid in layers. Power comes from the generating works of Vȳsōs and from the fuel drawn by the extraction stations above the gas giants Vermitos and Vagus, under the Magistracy of Vēzkostio, held in reserve against failure. The data centres are joined by a secure internal network kept wholly apart from the public network the realm's subjects use. Foundries, maintenance depots and the recycling of spent automatons answer to the Magistracy of Sētegsȳzi, fed by a chain of materials, automated in its simpler stages, that runs from the extraction stations on Taēsār and Merāeksys through the refineries to the foundries, and back again by recycling. Freight between Vȳsōs, its Moon, the colony on Vēzperzyon and the stations of the Vēzos system moves under the Magistracy of Naenierēba, its loading and routing increasingly given to automatons. Formation keeps its workshops, simulation halls and offices of ratification. A registry of every automaton, with standards of certification and rules of liability, is kept under the Magistracy of Vettsīrdārdrīvo. Defence against intrusion and tampering falls to the Gūrēñilaksi Lendārion and to a modest listening station on Morghūl.

The inspectorate keeps a chain of its own. Its automatons are made in its own foundries and trained on its own data, wholly apart from the builders', for a checker made in the builder's factory would be no independent check at all.

The Common Floor#

The means of production of the age of the Tireless Hand (its automatons, foundries and data centres) are held by the realm as a nationalised corporation. Its actions are voted upon by the representatives of the people, and it is ordered in tiers as the Five Governances are: the production of a township or city answers to that place's Gerialbar, the production of a world to that world's, and the great works of the realm to the Giezverde. In this manner the means of production are held in common and directed by those whom the people have chosen. It is run by professional managers, who count as part of the civil service and answer to the mandates of the representatives; and it is organised both by the levels of governance and by the services it provides. Each level of the corporation is bound first to the needs of its own Gerialbar; beyond those needs, it is free to pursue growth.

The realm's key public services (education, healthcare, network connectivity, housing, utilities and transport) are nationalised fully, provided outright or heavily subsidised, and furnished in part by the corporation's returns. These form the common floor beneath every Vysoan. What a Vysoan labours towards is not the means of living but what lies above it: luxuries, and improvements upon what is provided. The corporation, for its part, manages those goods where a measure of competition and slight scarcity is healthy. Within the realm it competes chiefly with other Vysoan firms, the contest lying in which has the better method and the better algorithm. Beyond the realm there is as yet no market to contend in, for Vysos has met no other people; its charter nonetheless provides for the day the corporation must compete with foreign firms to furnish whatever goods and services the peoples of the stars may desire.

What counts as basic is no fixed sum but a standard, revised periodically and kept current with what a Vysoan needs to live. Beside the blanket provision stands a means-testing, made extremely efficient by the realm's systems, so that those who require additional aid neither fall through the cracks nor are left stranded at a provision that does not meet their need. Such testing asks little the realm does not already know: wages, the number in a household, the place of residence, and the like.

The law provides that any newcomer who becomes naturalised shall be accorded the same entitlements as any Vysoan. The road to naturalisation it lays down, however, is long and steep, for adapting to Vysoan society would ask of a newcomer a considerable recalibration.

The provinces and worlds of the realm are kept equal not by equalising their outcomes but by governing them under one system, allocating benefits and entitlements to each by the same rules. Every province, from the Pryjatājoni at the realm's heart to the young colony on Vēzperzyon, is thus given the same launchpad and the same ability to excel. An equal outcome is held neither viable nor necessary, for whatever inequality remains between them is measured in access to luxuries and exclusive crafts, never in the essentials of living.

Housing, whose need predictive statistics have long struggled to estimate, is planned by thinking machines refined over the century and more of the realm's use of them. They meet need closely, and at the least maintain a standing surplus able to absorb sudden spikes in demand; where a shortfall arises in one place, surplus elsewhere is reallocated to meet it.

With necessities provided and machine-made goods growing ever cheaper, scarcity and competition move toward what machines cannot produce: handicraft, and the work of organic hands, valued for the very fact that a person made it.

Coin and Revenue#

The realm's vaults have kept pace with everything else the age has built. Vēzqelde, coin and bar in the realm's earlier centuries, is by RŌĀ 1017 a digital currency in every transaction an ordinary Vysoan actually makes, while the physical gold that has always stood behind it is neither retired nor much advertised, held whole in the Crown's own reserves rather than in any vault a depositor could reach. Its code, VĒQ, is set down already for the day it is listed on whatever exchanges the realm finds among the stars. The Treasury has also set down the rule by which Vēzqelde is to meet any foreign currency: such a currency is to be recognised plainly as a store of value, welcome at any Vysoan border and reckoned honestly against Vēzqelde rather than refused or discounted, but a purchase of Vysoan goods, or a stake in anything Vysoan, is to settle in Vēzqelde and nothing else, the visitor's money converted at the prevailing rate in the same instant the purchase is made.

The Crown is paid for by no single stream. The Crown lives chiefly on what it owns: the income of the old demesnes the Treasury collects, the berthing and transit dues of the realm's ports and orbital docks, the vaults' fees, and the royalties of every refinery, mine and extraction station worked under Crown licence, with a flat levy on the profit of corporations operating on Vysoan ground. Beside these runs a progressive levy on subjects' own earnings, light at its lowest bands and rising with income — the realm asking most of those its order has most rewarded.

Certainty for Sale#

Vysos does not yet know what peoples the stars hold, nor how they build or keep their machines. What it means to offer them, as it enters the galaxy, is not its machines but the system of checks that makes them trustworthy: the inspection and certification of other powers' automatons, so that a Vysoan seal passes as a mark of reliability; construction by Vysoan automaton crews under Vysoan inspection and ratification; automated docks, refuelling and repair yards along whatever lanes Vysoan ships come to ply; automated escort craft under organic Vysoan officers; automated clearing and settlement backed by the Crown's long stability; secure storage and computation in centres built for clients; and the training of foreign officials as checkers and ratifiers. Free of organic labour's costs, and with failures caught before they reach the client, such services are meant to undercut organic labour wherever they are offered.

Four rules are laid down to guard the advantage. Vysos is to lease and never sell: the core minds of its automatons stay within the realm, as the method of Vȳsōmēdon is kept a state secret. Client data is never to share the undisclosed centres that hold the realm's own memory. Vysos is to export no autonomous lethal force, for to sell abroad what the realm forbids at home would betray its own law. And whom it serves, and on what terms, is to be governed by whatever posture the realm takes toward the powers it meets.

Whether an automaton's mind may one day be carried from one body into another is a question no Vysoan workshop has yet answered, but the doctrine already prepares for it. Should such a transfer become possible, its memories, learned skills and character are to be drawn out under seal, inspected for completeness and for any foreign code, set into the new body, tested against the record of the original, and certified, with a backup held, if the client wishes, in the centres built for clients. An automaton without personal capacity may be copied into as many bodies as its owner wishes, for there is no person in it to be multiplied. And Vysos is to read no client automaton's memory beyond what the integrity of a transfer requires; this the realm undertakes to guarantee.

Should automatons ever come to hold a developed personality — a thing the realm's rudimentary thinking machines do not approach — the doctrine has sketched a further house of services for them: restoration workshops that repair without wiping, under the inspectorate's certificate; ateliers of bespoke bodies, the finest of them made by organic hands; maintenance havens along the lanes for automatons that travel with their owners; continuity vaults for memory and personality; and archives of honour, which would keep whole the mind of an automaton at the end of its service rather than scrap it. To these are to be joined the assessment and certification of personality, upgrades of skill and knowledge that leave the personality undisturbed, standards of keeping for those who own or lease such automatons, and placement with households, ships and employers suited to them.

Crowning these aims is the Vysoan Standard, by which the realm means to keep a measure of how work ought to run. It is the method of The Hand Remembered made ready for other peoples, backed by a thousand years of the realm's own records of how processes succeed and how they fail. A process bearing the Vysoan certification is attested on three counts: that it is efficient, achieving its purpose without waste, idle steps or needless burden on those who run it; that it is effective, reliably producing what it claims, as verified by the independent inspectorate; and that it is resilient, its reasons recorded, its people still able to run it by hand and its drills proving as much, so that it would survive the failure of its own machines. A lesser standard would attest that a process works today. The Vysoan Standard attests that it will still work when its machines do not.

The Standard states principles and leaves practice to its holder, for the realm's own system was calibrated for Vysoans and could not be carried whole to other peoples. What it learns of a client's operations in the course of certification is held under the same seal as any other client's data. It is the independence of the inspectorate, built and trained apart from the corporation, that lets the realm certify the processes of firms its own corporation competes with.

The Hand Remembered#

The realm holds that skill decays when it is not used, and that the Tireless Hand removes exactly the daily use that sustains it. Every work given over to automatons is therefore governed by a discipline of retention, so that Vysoans remain able to check what the machines do, to take over when they fail, and to understand why each work is done as it is. That discipline rests on three measures: every work is classified by the gravity of its failure, the hand-off of a work is barred until its worker has mastered it by hand, and short practice by hand continues for as long as the machines perform it.

Above all of it stands one governing rule: think first. Before consulting any thinking machine on a matter of judgement, a Vysoan first sets down a view of their own, namely the conclusion, the two or three reasons that carry it and what would change their mind. Only then do they consult the machine, asking it to critique that view as well as to answer, compare the two, decide, and record where they differed. The rule's depth scales with the order of the work, from a single line before a choice of procedure to a written view before any question of design or policy. It ensures that the organic remains the author of every judgement, and the machine its challenger.

No work is handed to the machines while the reason for any of its steps is unknown. Its keepers first record the work as it is actually done; ask of every step what fails if it is skipped, questioning the longest-serving hands and searching old records; ask those the step serves; and restate the purpose of the work as a whole. Each step is then sorted. A step whose reason is found and still valid is kept and its reason written down. One whose reason has passed is retired, and the cause recorded. One whose reason cannot be found is treated as possibly load-bearing, and is changed only on a small scale with a hand-performed fallback until what it guarded against is known.

Every work is classified by two independent measures. Its gravity is the consequence if the machines err or stop: grave works touch lives, money, the realm's obligations or confidences, and are hard to undo; weighty works are costly but caught further on; routine works are minor and easily reversed. Its order is the level of the work the machines take over, rising through six orders: direct action; diagnosis and procedure; sequencing and coordination; design and integration; the coherence of a whole enterprise; and the shaping of the realm's place among its neighbours. In the first order the machines execute. In the second they suggest and the organic decides. In the third they build and optimise while the organic sets the constraints. From the fourth upward no work is ever wholly given over: the machine drafts, analyses and challenges, but the organic remains its author. A work is classified by the work the machines took over, not by the checking that remains, and where its measures are in doubt the higher is taken. At RŌĀ 1017 the realm's machines hold works of the first and second orders, and only a few of the third; the rules for the higher orders stand ready for a reach the machines have not yet gained.

A newcomer performs every grave and weighty work by hand until passing its gate, which ends when the work is mastered, not after a fixed span of days. An experienced hand first performs the work aloud, saying why each step exists. The newcomer then performs it with the written procedure and is asked of every step what fails without it, and works through at least one exception or deliberately seeded error. The gate is passed only when, at least a week after training has ended, the newcomer performs the work to standard on three consecutive realistic cases including one exception, explains why each step exists, spots an error seeded in a machine's output, and runs the hand-performed fallback. The machines then run in shadow while the newcomer verifies every output, for four weeks in grave works and two in weighty ones. Routine works need only a walkthrough of what the machines do and why. Those who already know a work by hand take its gate once before it is handed over. In this the gate carries into working life the formation in which every Vysoan first learns to do by hand what the machines will later do.

Once a work is handed over, two kinds of practice continue. The machines' outputs are verified according to gravity: a sample of grave works each month, weighty works each quarter, and routine works only on exception. Skill is kept by drills according to order, rising in frequency as the work grows more complex and held one step more often for grave works: from a yearly drill in simple grave works to twice a year in the higher orders. Every drill requires the reason of each step to be stated, and from the second order upward it includes an exception or a seeded error. Drills are also called whenever a work or its machines change, an error escapes the checks, a Vysoan returns to a work after six months away, or a work faces unusual load. They rotate among the workers, so that no work rests on one memory; they are recorded; and they take minutes, not hours, so that the Tireless Hand still saves the labour it was given to save. The realm requires no generic exercises of the mind: the only practice that keeps a skill alive is the skill itself.

The independent inspectorate checks the work of the automatons. The organic overseer of a work checks it too, and the realm does not assign a second organic to check the first. Two aids make this sufficient. The first is a short set of three to seven guiding questions, shown at the very point of checking, each aimed at an error a quick glance would miss, each carrying its reason in one line, framed as questions rather than ticks, and revised from the record of exceptions so that they never harden into ritual. The second is a single register of where every work's knowledge lives, for what a Vysoan seldom performs will fade from memory, and what must not fade is knowing where to find it. No work goes live until its record holds eight things: its steps with their reasons; what the machines do; the hand-performed fallback; a record of exceptions and of the reasoning behind workarounds; practice cases on dummy records; its keeper, gravity and drill record; its guiding questions; and its entry in the register. A missing item bars the hand-over.

A change to a work, or a failure of its machines, is treated as a lesson as well as a repair. When a work changes, its workers are shown the old step beside the new and told why, and in grave works they pass the gate again before the change goes live. When the machines fail, the written fallback is run at the point of work, since under strain the mind recalls little and falls back on habit. A short debrief within the week asks what was expected, what happened, why and what changes, and the case enters the record of exceptions and the practice cases.

The realm guards against the quieter ways in which skill erodes. At least two Vysoans pass the gate of every grave work, and knowledge is taught, not merely shadowed, at every hand-over. Each quarter a known error is planted in a live sample to prove that the checkers still check. Drills are without penalty, and forgetting is held to be expected rather than shameful, so that no one hides what they have lost. Once a year each grave work is run by hand for a full week, to prove that the realm could bear a long outage and not merely a brief one. The reasons recorded for grave works are revalidated each year and whenever a governing rule changes. Drill time is counted as a running cost of every machine, so that no economy is found in cutting it, and a sample of drills is audited each year, with the catching of seeded errors taken as the proof. Should Vysos one day certify or build for foreign clients, the doctrine requires that it be the clients' own people, not Vysoan crews, who pass each gate before hand-over. Any reason a machine proposes for a step remains a hypothesis until a person confirms it.

The drill records are the realm's evidence for refining the discipline. A drill passed without its reasons counts as only a partial pass, because the steps and their reasons are distinct and both decay. Learning is judged after a delay, never at the end of instruction. Where a work's drills show no error for two consecutive cycles, its interval is lengthened by a step; where they show error, it is shortened.

Culture & Daily Life

What Vysos Eats#

The court table keeps Old Zobrezos cuisine largely unchanged — seafood in citrus and spice, a raw-fish delicacy, roasted meat brought in from the mainland, bread, rice, and millet, a spiced soup, sweet-spiced wine — layered over with colonial luxuries picked up over time. The common table, never given a High Vysoan name, is the true unification dish: the steamed, herbed grain of Ghisazma as universal staple, a salt-sweet spiced pepper stew blending a Pelarton base with Āerakii pepper as the unity dish, Sȳndorīa's sweet roast meats and steamed fish-with-greens kept distinct rather than blended in, fruit shaved ice with sweet honey jelly for dessert, and a sweet wine as the one universal favorite. The colony on Vēzperzyon and the extraction stations of the Vēzos system eat food shipped up from Vȳsōs, since agriculture stays strictly on the homeworld by standing policy (see History); fleet and Scion rations are sealed, vacuum-packed common-table meals.

The Course of a Life#

Beyond schooling, a Vysoan life runs a fairly fixed course across its eighty-odd years. Majority arrives at 25 with a tertiary credential — and, for a Maegystīrys holder, the vote together with it — though standing for office is left for later, once a subject has genuinely lived among the consequences of the system he'd propose to run. Work begins at once, in a corporation or the civil service, and marriage follows around 30 — not a romantic institution but a formal partnership judged on how well two people work together and whether they and their families share a vision for the future; genuine political candidacy tends to arrive in the same decade. The nobility marry earlier, their pool of eligible houses being smaller. The working decades that follow are shaped by a belief that a position is a role the realm needs filled, not proof of the holder's worth against anyone else's — a subject with the disposition climbs, while one who finds his level settles there and optimizes rather than strains upward, neither path ranked above the other. A second flowering, a genuine mid-life career change, is normal rather than eccentric in the forties, and capstone service — senior civil, magisterial, or military appointment — typically runs through the fifties and sixties. Retirement proper is customarily set at 70, and the years it opens are spent at leisure and in conveying accumulated wisdom to the young. The custom is kept firmly for office but loosely for everything else: a subject still vigorous past seventy no longer holds an appointment, yet may go on teaching, counselling and keeping the records of the work he once did, and is sought out for it. None of this touches the Crown itself: a Kardārys recognizes no retirement or abdication, reigning for life, with incapacity alone opening the throne to a regency (see History) rather than a chosen succession.

When the Light Does Not Return#

The realm's physicians can hold a body's own life functions running long past any hope of the mind behind them returning — a condition the Covenant names apart from both death and continuing life, reasoning from its own solar theology that a subject is the capacity to receive the Starshaper's light rather than the body's mere persistence, so a body kept warm past that light's return is read as a lamp tended after its flame has gone out. Confirmation is never medical alone: a physician's finding is attended and confirmed by clergy trained in the Covenant's own discernment, a brief bedside rite of witness rather than a signature, and for the Crown itself that confirmation must be joined by a witness from the Solar Scions' own Ūndissari before any regency is understood to have opened. Once confirmed the subject is reckoned dead for every purpose the record keeps, dated from the rite rather than from whatever moment the sustained body eventually stops, and extraordinary measures are withdrawn as a matter of course — continuing them past confirmation is read less as mercy than as a quiet impiety, keeping a doused lamp lit for those still holding it.

What the Vat Cannot Grow#

Vysoan physicians have only lately learned to grow simple tissues — skin, cartilage, the lining of a vessel — from a subject's own cells, and whole organs remain beyond them; replacement, where it can be had at all, still comes by donation from another subject. The Covenant has nonetheless already settled which it prefers: grown flesh remains one's own record continuing, where donated flesh carries a stranger's witnessed life folded quietly in, so that as the art matures it is to become the ordinary recourse and donation the rarer one. None of it would arrest aging: the capacity to receive the Starshaper's light is seated in the mind rather than in any part a vat could grow, and a mind cannot be replaced without producing someone else, so even a body whose machinery could be renewed without end would still carry a witness behind the eyes that cannot be — its own slow wearing is what aging and death have always actually been. The realm accordingly expects no art of the vat to unsettle the course of a life above; at most it may let a subject meet the end of that course in better health.

The Realm's Letters#

Only a small handful of works have crossed from record into lasting classic, set down here in the order they were written. The eldest of them by a wide margin is Ikarvēttīlaksir — The Great Game — a sprawling historical drama written sometime during the reign of Āelyxanthor himself, the Founder (RŌĀ 36–81), chronicling the final unraveling of an older order entirely, generations before the realm itself was raised: the forty families of the Zaldrāeksi at the height of their quarrels at its opening, and Valiērīa's capital and core swallowed by the Cataclysm at its close, its dragonlords' long rivalries left unfinished by a ruin none of them had foreseen. Its author's name has not survived; tradition guesses at a chronicler from the fallen empire's own order of record-keepers, though nothing beyond guesswork has ever been proven. It was set down in the very reign the Founder was raising Zobrezos upon the Pryjatājoni from what the fallen empire had left behind, and has been read ever since as the realm's account of what it rose from.

The eldest work written after the Founder's reign, and the most private of them, is Vāedarvāedarie — Heart of Hearts, its superlative built the same reduplicating way the throne's own style later builds Dārysdāri, King of Kings — a sequence of passionate poems written by Ēlyāegon in the long years before his own unlooked-for ascent, a nephew with no particular claim on the throne who did not inherit it from his uncle until nine-and-fifty. They are cast as letters in verse to a single beloved who is never named and never answers, following one courtship through the turning of thirteen months, from the first meeting at the Jemēsiñ Vēzose to its anniversary a year on. History remembers Ēlyāegon I as "the Enlightened," the king whose reign first harnesses steam and founds a line that will hold the crown unbroken for some hundred and sixty years from his accession; Vāedarvāedarie is the quiet correction to that reputation — a man practiced in feeling before he was ever called to rule. It shares that distinction, and very nearly its own years of composition, with a soldier's private reckoning written under two kings before Ēlyāegon I's own reign had begun.

That soldier's book is Otāpatrūmirī — Reckonings Kept Between Campaigns — written by Taēmor Vaelaris, a Vysoan military commander and philosopher who served through the reigns of Aurys and Dāeriōñ , the thirteen years of war that put down Pelarton's Braedhōs-backed revolt and the treaty that ended it. Set down between campaigns rather than at leisure, it is kept as a ledger rather than a guide: each entry weighs one campaign's cost in lives, grain and broken towns against the oath that commanded it, and asks plainly whether the debt was owed, the commander never sparing his own orders from the reckoning. It is read ever after as a companion to Vāedarvāedarie rather than a rival to it, a king and an officer setting their private thoughts to the page within the same span of years, neither aware of the other's. Between them, the two stand as the oldest attested works written after the Founder's reign; only Ikarvēttīlaksir, set down while the Founder himself still reigned, is older.

Gōstikos, written at the newly founded Maegysombāzmion under Ēlyrōz , "the Erudite" (RŌĀ 393–405), well over a century after those two, is not a chronicle of anything that had already happened but an attempt to reason out what might keep the realm intact across centuries its author never expected to see — closer to grand strategy turned into private speculation than to any of the realm's other letters. Its title has never been translated to general satisfaction and is simply kept as given.

Younger than Gōstikos by barely a generation, and the first practical manual of its own kind rather than a speculation, is Otāpahae Ēlvalys — Thoughts Set Down for a Prince — written under Kēlāethor , whose eight-year reign was spent almost entirely putting down one contending princeling after another, by Naekarlos Maegivalys, an important Zobrezi official and one of that king's own closest counselors. Rather than chronicle the crisis, Maegivalys distilled it into a method for outlasting one — how a prince holds a contested throne by patience rather than terror, binds the factions he cannot yet master into offices and law until their ambitions run in the Crown's service, and keeps a court that would rather see him fail too busy with its own advancement to arrange it — and it remains the realm's founding work of statecraft, much of early Vysoan governance tracing back to it. The Maegivalys line, ennobled for the book, has held significant government office for some six centuries since, several heirs rising to Dēmōndosēr, First Minister to the Throne.

The realm's oldest work of invented-world narrative — none of its elders had yet set a tale entirely apart from the realm's own history — is Vīlībāz Rōzdaor — The Nameless War — by Jaenon Thorkyn, known by the single name Thorkyn, a subject of mixed High and Common Vysoan blood and no particular house who served as a junior officer in Rāeōñ 's war against Sȳndorīa, the bloodiest campaign the Vēzgharyōñs had yet fought for a peace that changed no border worth drawing. He spent the better part of a decade after his return folding that experience, transfigured almost past recognition, into an invented age of his own — two kingdoms locked for generations in a war whose cause neither any longer remembers, and the small company of common soldiers, drawn from both sides, sent across a ruined continent to recover the treaty-roll on which the quarrel was first written, only to find at the journey's end that it was never written at all — publishing the result late in Rāeōñ I's reign and living to see it read into the reign of Rāeōñ I's son, Rāethor , who named him Valzantys, a knight, for the book as much as for the war behind it. It flatters no throne and glorifies no war, and remains the standard against which every Vysoan epic written since has been measured. Thorkyn's heirs kept building on the work across the generations that followed, and the house they raised on its renown rose in turn to Pāleqiros, Companion of the Crown, by RŌĀ 1017.

Isēgeves Vīlībāzmae, credited to a commander who served under Āedāriōñ and set it down as Āeñāriōñ came to the throne in RŌĀ 1017 — the same reign in which the Vysoan military is being settled into its present configuration — is doctrine stripped bare rather than reflection: terrain, formation, and the calculated cost of a battle weighed before it is fought. Already taken up at the Botȳsombāzmion and the Maegysombāzmion alike, it is valued for the clarity of its thinking rather than for any one victory it can claim.

Beyond the Page#

Vysoan letters were not confined to the page forever. Aerēbai Rȳqelosie — Journeys Among the Stars — is the earliest attested departure from it: a science-fiction epic written for broadcast rather than for binding, following a series of starship captains and their crews across an imagined galaxy of strange worlds and stranger company, aired to Vysoan screens under Vēzāeriōñ , "the Stargazer" (RŌĀ 858–885), the same king whose own reign, having run out of frontier to conquer on Vȳsōs itself, plants the house's first foothold on the Moon. No proof that such company exists anywhere beyond Vȳsōs has reached the realm even now — Aerēbai Rȳqelosie's alien crews were invented whole, imagined by a people with every reason to suppose themselves alone, and whether they are alone is a question the realm has only begun to put: a single test vessel has made the first jump, and the first drive-fitted ships, begun under Āedāriōñ , are still building.

Sētegos Idārys — To Make a King — turns the oldest succession crisis in the realm's history into theater: the twenty-eight-year civil war between Āeñāriōñ and his sister Āelyxaena that nearly ended the line, staged the better part of two and a half centuries after the fact under Ēlyrōz (RŌĀ 393–405), the same reign and royal patronage of learning that produces Gōstikos. Its title borrows the realm's own craft vocabulary — Sēteg-, the root behind Sētegombāzmion, the Guildhall, and Sētegtīrys, Certified Craftmaster — turned toward the one thing Vysoan succession law insists can never be crafted, only inherited. The play takes no side between brother and sister, lingering instead on the lesser claimants and the commons caught between their armies, whom a less patient chronicle would have let history forget.

Zaldrāeksi — The Dragonlords — is the newest work of the chapter by a wide margin, produced for Vysoan screens in RŌĀ 1017 itself: a costume drama of the forty families who ruled Valiērīa, their dragons, their marriages and their rivalries, set at the height of the empire rather than at its end. Where Ikarvēttīlaksir keeps its players nameless and its gaze on the ruin, Zaldrāeksi names all forty houses and follows them through the long centuries of their greatness, leaving the Cataclysm itself to Ikarvēttīlaksir's own account of it, set down far closer to the fact. House Vēzgharyōñ stands among the forty, but the drama keeps it to the margins of the tale — one family among many, not yet the line that would outlast the rest.

What Vysos Wears#

Civilian dress reads as the Crown's own vestments inherited downward, graded by rank rather than birth. Men wear a sleek, dark, metallic-trimmed tunic cinched by a wide sash, under a cloak cut to fasten rather than merely drape — pinned at the right shoulder with a jewelled clasp — its lining (plain, gold-shot, or oxblood) marking status. Women wear a draped floor-length gown beneath a long, patterned band of cloth crossing the body diagonally from shoulder to hem, its woven — not dyed — motifs immediately legible as house and province, absorbed provinces' own patterns persisting within the shared silhouette rather than being erased. A common variant, no less proper, fits the bodice close beneath a high standing collar and lets the band fall straight from a broad belt rather than crossing the body, the fullness kept to the skirt and the handwork to collar, cuffs, belt and hem. Both sexes wear sun-gold jewelry scaled to rank; ruby and fire opal mark piety and old blood, emerald marks descent from the forty families of the Zaldrāeksi, and pink tourmaline marks new colonial wealth — the one gem the old nobility of the Pryjatājoni never had.

The line of Vysoan dress is a long, close-fitted coat, falling straight and narrow to the knee or calf, fastened down the front and closed at the throat by a high standing collar. Its plain body is left to the machine's precision; its collar, cuffs and front edge are the natural seats of the wearer's handwork. It is worn in many colours, not one: grey, blue, black, deep red and others besides, each set off by gold handwork, so that a Vysoan crowd is varied rather than uniform. The realm's restraint lies in how ornament is handled, never in a single prescribed colour.

Over it falls a long cloak, a common element of Vysoan dress worn day to day as well as on occasions and in office, in a cut handed down from the old court of Zobrezos: sweeping cleanly from the shoulders to the heel, lightly structured rather than heavy, its borders worked by hand. Vysoan custom keeps its own fastening and lining rules for it, the clasp at the right shoulder and the lining marking status.
